Mr. Speaker, in that case I would like to say that for the opposition it is not a matter of objecting to a bill like this one which provides so little. We want to take this opportunity to make it clear to Canadians that for a government that for seven years has been promising Canadians it would tighten up the judicial system, it has actually done very little.
In fact, many comments from non-partisan sources imply that nothing will change and that no major changes will be made as a result of the bill before the House.

We cannot support the bill without making it clear to the Government of Canada how much we object to their failure to deal with serious problems within the criminal justice system of our country.
When I was Solicitor General I had the honour to propose and sponsor the first crime prevention week in Canada. I watched the program grow during our administration to make a very worth-while contribution to reducing the amount of crime in Canadian society.
I was also the first Solicitor General to devote funds to support victims. I called for the first victims' conference which took place-I still remember all of it very well-in the Park Plaza Hotel in the city of Toronto in 1980.
From that event a tremendous amount of understanding developed of the plight of the victim in the criminal justice system. This bill makes a very small addition to the measures we previously had to bring victims to a sense of justice in the development of the criminal justice system. I am not going to focus on the shortcomings and the smoke and mirrors that are contained in this bill. I have something much more important to say about what it is that the government is trying to do with this bill.
It is trying to make this small package of very little look like a method of fighting crime and reducing the amount of crime in Canadian society. While this bill may reduce some victimization that would otherwise take place without this bill, of all of those who are accused of crimes in Canada less than 2 per cent end up in federal penitentiaries. When they are released the great majority of that 2 per cent do not reoffend, whether they are on parole or not.
If the government wants Canadians to think that this is a measure that is going to do something about crime, I want people to realize that this bill does very little. This government has done very little in areas where we can

November 5, 1991

make great strides in reducing the amount of crime in Canadian society. In fact it has moved in a retrograde direction.
I want to talk about crime prevention week not only because I was its sponsor. It focuses on an area and on a series of techniques and programs which really do reduce the amount of victimization in Canadian society in a very measurable and remarkable way that does not always involve police action. In fact I want to talk about crime prevention measures which may not even have occurred to this Solicitor General or to his parliamentary secretary. They are measures that really do address the aberration in society which leads to crime. The government's focus is on that very small percentage of 2 per cent of those who run afoul of the criminal justice system.
Crime prevention week focused on such programs as neighbourhood watch which keeps track of households when families are away from them. It focused on many other programs and drew on volunteer participation. It is now going to be abandoned by this federal government because it says other levels of government can take it over now.
I want to make the point that this is just another example of our national government, the Mulroney government, abandoning an area of authority and responsibility that Canadians want to be very involved in.
When you ask Canadians what is special about Canada, they talk about some of our social programs, our safety net and so on but they also talk about the relatively low level of crime that we have known historically compared to other countries. That is changing and this bill is not going to reverse the trend, I can tell you that.
I think Canadians are proud of the low levels of crime in this country and they want their federal government to be identified with that. It is a national value in this country that we have historically kept crime at low levels. To hear the federal government say: "The provinces are happy to take this program over. We have no business doing it", is just one of the reasons why this country is in jeopardy. It is because we are not reinforcing our national strengths. We are not seeing the national resources used to preserve and strengthen the things that the Canadian people believe in.

The most successful crime prevention program in the history of the world-I would love to be able to say it is one that I introduced but it was not- is day care. I want members of the House to realize what an enormous opportunity was lost when this government broke its promise to deliver a day care program in this country based on need. The reason I can make such a dramatic statement about the impact that day care has on crime is because in the United States of America during President Johnson's administration, which in many ways does not get the recognition that it deserves, one of the so-called great society programs was Head Start. This program was begun in the early 1960s and it lasted for seven or eight years. It was offered in almost every population centre in the United States. Thousands and thousands of young people, many of them living in substandard living conditions, were brought into programs where they were given the opportunity to develop.
What is interesting about this program and why I mention it now is that the oldest of these young people are 35 and 36 years old. Important longitudinal studies have been made of these people who went through the program, tens of thousands of them all around the United States, comparing them to people who lived in similar circumstances but did not have the benefit of the Head Start program. There are enormous differences between Head Start young people and those deprived of that program in the amount of criminal activity in which they engage and the amount of all forms of deviant behaviour they contribute to: alcoholism, chronic joblessness, drug addiction, and more relevant to today, crime. The differences between that group of young Americans and the others is so categorically demonstrated that it is time for the government to recognize that crime prevention and fighting crime through crime prevention is infinitely more significant and also considerably less expensive than the kind of measures that are being proposed today.
This bill is barely worth having. It is being presented to the Canadian people as a way of dealing with crime but experts doubt it will make much of a difference. The program on which the government promised action and on which it broke its promises is a program which would really have worked to reduce the amount of crime in Canadian society.

Mr. Speaker, I have a few words to say on Bill C-36. It is on people's minds now because there has been an increase in crime including violent crime in places like Toronto.
This bill is not dealing with the whole question of crime though there is an argument that we should be doing that. However that is not actually the subject of the bill. The bill deals with violent criminal offenders.
This legislation would increase the length of time or the length of a sentence that such an offender would be required to spend in prison. It would increase the length of time from one-third of his sentence to one-half of his sentence. It would also add to the list of violent offenders certain new categories such as those who sexually molest children, arsonists and dangerous drug offenders. That means those who are serious ringleaders or kingpins in the drug industry.
The legislation would also improve the flow of information from the sentencing judge to the parole board so that the parole board would be aware of the facts about
Government Orders
the history of the offender whose sentence they are considering.
As has been pointed out I think that all sides of the House are in favour of this bill.
In principle.

The hon. member has said "in principle" and that means of course exactly what we are voting on at second reading, approval in principle. When it goes to committee then of course there will be discussion of details with the possibility of amendments.
This is not the time to talk about possible amendments. However I am concerned with the context of this bill, partly in the sense that has been mentioned by some previous speakers that this bill was a long time coming. But my main concern is that it could be taken, although it is not necessarily so intended, to suggest that more police, more convictions, more jails and more time in jail are the solutions to crime.
The increase in crime is not entirely an accident or a coincidence in our time. The increase in crime happens to come at a time of unemployment in the city of Toronto for example such as we have not had for decades. I am not just talking about high unemployment, but longterm unemployment. I have talked to people who have been hunting for jobs for two years. I do not mean sitting at home waiting for a job to come. I mean out there knocking on doors or telephoning in response to advertisements for two years.
That can do some damage to a person's spirit. I am not suggesting and nobody in this House is suggesting that it justifies the commission of a crime, whether it is a violent one or a non-violent one. What I am saying is that when we are concerned about an increase in crime we should examine the kind of things that contribute to the breakdown of a human spirit to the point where a person may-not everybody does-be more likely to commit a crime including possibly a violent crime.
For that reason I want to remind the government and the listening public including my city of Toronto that there are other things that are needed in order to address the apparent rising rate of crime. One is closely related to this although it is not part of the subject matter of the bill. It is the fact that by passing this law we

November 5, 1991
Government Orders
can ensure that certain prisoners will stay in prison longer than they did before. But they will come out, they will come out. We might give ourselves a bit of a breathing space before they come out. If we do not do anything useful with that breathing space it is not likely they will be any less dangerous when they do come out. If they are too dangerous to let out now and they stay in prison for months or years longer, we have no guarantee that they will be less dangerous. It is at least equally possible they might be more dangerous when they come out because prison is often called a school of crime, in whatever sense that may be meant.
Unless the time in prison is used for rehabilitation then it is likely that all we are doing is postponing the danger to the public that we would like to prevent or to reduce. That requires staff work.
I have read from time to time in the papers about some repeat violent offender who had received no kind of treatment for the nature of his previous offence while he was in prison. I am speaking mainly of men. He had received no treatment. There was not enough appropriate staff. There were no facilities and so on.
This could be regarded as a stopgap or a band-aid only. It will not serve the intended purpose unless in addition the government through the correction system provides a much more serious and solid rehabilitation program for offenders than we now have. This especially includes violent offenders.
But there are other matters also and this has been warned of long ago. When I was on Toronto city council and metro council during the 1970s people were warning then that the lack of adequate public support for child care would result in violence in a decade or so. The children were being sometimes poorly cared for because of their parents' poverty or because of in one-parent families, one parent, or in two-parent families, both parents, had to work away from the house for long hours. Latchkey children were being neglected. Children had a key to the apartment hung around their necks and were on their own when they went back home for lunch and when they came home after school.
People were warning about this. Metro council social services committee and the appropriate bodies of city
council addressed their warnings to the senior levels of government that neglecting children then would ensure that some of those would grow up to be criminals, even violent criminals, later on. That has to be given attention.
There is furthermore a rehabilitation of people who are addicted to drugs. I have had people come to my office begging for assistance for an adult son, for instance. He was a drug addict and according to medical information needed treatment in a residential treatment centre in Canada. But there were not enough beds in the centre. I have met a few of those but I know there are many more instances where a person wants treatment, needs residential treatment but cannot get it. He thereby continues to be addicted to some of these harmful drugs and becomes a dangerous offender or at least part of the pattern in which the dangerous offenders are created.
This government must give more attention to the cost of child care which is cheaper than the cost of criminal care and to the cost of drug rehabilitation before addicted people enter into the stream of violent crime.
Without attention to those programs, rehabilitation of the criminals, care of the children and rehabilitation of addicted persons, this bill we are approving today will be a deception and a trap. It will not prevent violence. It will only postpone it and quite possibly increase it.

Mr. Speaker, I wish to say a few words on Bill C-36, which is intended, in principle anyway, to restore public confidence in Canada's prison and parole system.
If one reads the bill carefully, the guiding principle of the new provisions is to protect the public first and foremost; that is the most important consideration in all matters relating to the release of offenders on parole. That is the purpose.
As a parliamentarian I must tell you that I am sorry the government waited seven years to present a bill like this one. I receive many calls and letters from my constituents on this subject. Not only have they lost confidence in the system, but they are quite reluctant to support the measures which the government is proposing in this bill.

Protecting the public is so important and the public has so many reasons to be concerned in our big cities and elsewhere that strong measures against criminals are justified. We are not mistaken; the facts are there. An article in Montreal's La Presse, I think last May, reported that violent crimes, murders, kidnappings, sexual and other assaults had increased steadily since 1977. They followed the general trend, increasing from 248,580 to 269,118 or 6.8 per cent. They now affect one person in a hundred, the highest rate in our history. It goes on to say that this type of crime now accounts for 10 per cent of all infractions committed throughout the country. The article tells us that the rising level of violence has now reached crisis proportions.
Strict measures must be put in place. I am absolutely convinced that unless we implement known measures which are strictly enforced by the judges and our correctional system, the problem will not be solved.

I had occasion to speak recently to somebody from the Ottawa police force because I was concerned about the violence in my riding.
Again last night we had a rape at an OC Transpo public place. It was a violent rape. The individual in question apparently was raped and then beaten.
This occurs pretty well every week now. People in my riding are responding. I want to read a few extracts from letters. I do not want to name the person because it is a confidence: "Why should the public have any confidence in a justice system when the rights of the convicted rapist takes precedence over the right of society to feel secure. Victims live in terror because of threats that they receive". Further on it says that while on parole many of these criminals repeat the same acts and again are let go too soon.
In the proposed legislation I must admit there are some good measures. There are also some things which we would like to see tightened up. I want to address the question of the hearing before the parole board for a criminal who wants to apply for his conditional release on parole.
At the present time, if I understand the system, a criminal is allowed after serving one-third of his sen-
Govemment Orders
tence to apply for a parole hearing. Under the proposed legislation before us a judicial determination can be made to extend that to half of the sentence. It would be up to a judge to say: "Yes, by our system, one is entitled to a parole hearing after one-third but in this case I determine that half the sentence must be served before this can be invoked". It would be up to a judge.
I am one of those who believe it should be automatic. There should be no release before one-half of the sentence. I am of the belief also that the victims of crime have rights and should be represented before that judge or before that parole board at the victim's discretion. It should not be at the discretion of a parole board. I asked the police force in the city of Ottawa today what they thought about that. They even went so far as to say: "If the victim does not want to appear then he or she could have representation on his or her behalf before this hearing as a right so that they would be kept informed of what is happening in this criminal case".
I would hope the government would seek to amend the legislation and put the automatic requirements in the bill. Having said that, I would like to repeat what I said at the beginning. We are indeed very preoccupied with the present system. It is failing many of us. It is failing our daughters and our sons. It is failing our elderly citizens. It is creating fear in the system. I can give untold examples in my own riding of Ottawa-Vani-er of people living in fear today because of a violent experience they had and because they do not have the information that they would like to have or they should have in regard to the justice system reserved for those who are found guilty of criminal acts.
I would hope that the government would tighten up this bill and put in it the rights of the victims just as seriously and with just as much care as they have at this time considered the rights of the criminals.

Mr. Speaker, I take the opportunity to join my colleagues in debating at second reading the parole legislation which is before us. I do this, as other members have done, because not only is the issue of crime a serious one in Canadian society, generally speaking, but it is an issue that unfortunately is on the climb. It is on the climb in terms of the illegal

November 5, 1991
Government Orders
series of violent crimes in our communities. It is also up in terms of the conscience of a community.
I have public meetings at least once a month in my community. I have participated in the various municipal election campaigns that are currently under way in Ontario. As you speak to people in these public forums and at their homes, the issue of so-called law and order and the issue of coming to grips with the crime element in our communities is very pervasive.
I would categorize the complaints and the frustrations coming from our citizens in the community of York West into three areas: first, the element of criminal activity is up particularly in terms of the illicit drug trade in our community. Second, there is a feeling of frustration that many judicial decisions coming from our benches are too lax. With all due respect to our criminal system, they are too lax in terms of facing the real problem. The third item concerns the illicit drug trade. The profits or proceeds from a number of those drug busts that come from the local police authorities and local organizations that are engaged on the front lines should go back to general revenues at the federal government level which are very distant from the front line battles. This should be used to try to come to grips with fighting the illegal drug trade in our communities.
There is a great deal of frustration with those three points, particularly the last point. In concert with our Solicitor General critic who has started a national petition across the country, I have tried to distribute this petition far and wide to come to grips with the situation of drug profits. When we do make one of those busts those profits should be shared with our local police forces and our local organizations which are responsible for trying to win this battle. If crime is a serious problem then it cries out for serious solutions. We cannot have a serious problem and then simply pick a week where, as a public relations exercise, we try to somehow convince the public that the government is doing something about it when in fact it clearly is not.
We have waited for this particular legislation for seven years. The government has had ample opportunity to come to grips with the particular problems plaguing the parole system of Canada. Yet not only has it taken seven years but this is the third time it has announced that it is going to do something about it.
The last time was on the eve of the 1988 federal election campaign. I would submit with all due respect it is that type of a charade that is bleeding public credibility for this government and for politicians and institutions across this land.
If it is a serious problem then let us come to grips with it in this Chamber, this government and across the country and do something about it. We have waited seven years and the promise has been reworked three times in order to maximize it in terms of political credibility. I believe that Canadians are not that gullible.
This is crime prevention week and for the first time since 1983 the government has walked away from participating financially in sustaining the awareness level of crime in our country during this one week. If there was ever a time for a national government to participate in trying to promote awareness, this was the year. Yet the government walked away from it.
You have to ask if the government is serious about coming to grips with this problem. Is it simply satisfied to fill up a number of hours on a Tuesday, followed up by another number of bills, wash its hands and then move on to the next agenda item?
I would suggest that the government must do what it says it is going to do not only now but in the future and not inflate the rhetoric.
In the few minutes accorded to me I would like to draw on some of the highlights of the actual piece of legislation. The government says that this legislation will actually serve to protect the public in terms of it being paramount.
Right off the bat I would have assumed along with my other colleagues on this side that public safety would be issue number one in the current legislation. We do not have to get new legislation to suggest that public safety all of a sudden is going to be priority number one. That begs the question: Where has public safety been up until now, after seven years of this government's rule? That speaks to the very malaise and the very frustration people in our communities feel. Somehow public safety and the safety of our communities is far down the list.
Therefore off the top of this government's list, the paramountcy of public safety ought to be issue number one in our current operations without even discussing the new Bill C-36.

The second aspect is that it is, for the first time, trying to formally recognize the victims of crime. The government is suggesting that the victims of crime would be allowed to attend a parole hearing at the discretion of the parole board rather than at the discretion of the offender. Obviously at the discretion of the offender is a non-starter. We are saying, why not go all the way? If you are interested in public safety, if you are interested in recognizing that somehow the victims of crime must also be thought about, then why not make that opportunity automatic? Why not leave it to the victims of crime to decide for themselves and for their families whether they wish to choose to exercise the right of appearing at that hearing in order to make a salient point about the offender. Rather than placing the onus of choice on the parole officer, we are suggesting victims of crime be given the automatic right to defend and promote their own concerns first hand at the parole hearings or at least to designate someone to do it on their behalf.
That is another measure that is seen by our side as a half measure. We are going to promote in committee that we go all the way and recognize those victims of crime who unfortunately are all too often the forgotten variable in this ugly equation called crime.
Another aspect of a half measure is that the government purports to introduce judicial determination. This will give judges the opportunity to lengthen the time spent in prison to at least half rather than one-third the term for violent offenders and serious drug offenders. If the Government of Canada really wants a crackdown, then let us make that automatic. Let us not have that as a potential possibility for judges because there will be different judges in different parts of the country taking different views. I believe we ought to have some national standards about the wave of crime across this country.
We are suggesting that those offenders be automatically made to serve at least half of their sentence, otherwise it becomes a mockery.
The last point is the suggestion that first-time offenders, largely white collar criminals, be given a provision called accelerated review. This would accelerate their
Government Orders
parole as compared to the more violent criminals in our society. We will have to think carefully about that. While there may be different variations of crime we also have to be careful about the standards that we are suggesting.
Are we suggesting that we have a double standard? There would be one for blue collar crime, perhaps out in our communities. There would be another for white collar crime that may take place in some office tower. It may in fact be the lynch pins and controlling individuals who support this kind of activity.
I am suggesting that yes, we have a problem with overcrowding in our jails. What price are we going to pay in order to solve that, by suggesting that white collar crime is less important than blue collar crime? I am suggesting that we should standardize that. For those who are supporting white collar crime, they must bear the price of society as well.
I notice that you are indicating that my time is up. I look forward to speaking on this bill once again in committee stage and at third reading.

Mr. Speaker, blue skies are now visible over Kuwait again, thanks to the efforts of two oil fire fighting teams from Alberta who helped put out the 732 oil well fires set by Saddam Hussein's army.
This task took only 10 months, instead of the predicted two to three years. The success of these Canadians has made a significant contribution to ending the ecological trauma that these oil fires represented to the environment and to rebuilding Kuwaiti oil production.
Putting out oil well fires is an endeavour of refined experience which combines science and raw courage. The Canadian oil patch has contributed to oil exploration recovery and safety all around the world: Texas, Oklahoma, Middle East, Indonesia and the North Sea are some of the areas.
The two Alberta teams from Safety Boss of Calgary and Red Flame of Red Deer are part of this proud tradition and Canadians are proud of them for their work. We congratulate them and welcome them home.

Mr. Speaker, it has come to light with the closure of the Wolverine Copper Thbe plant in Delta that the company and, to a lesser extent, others have been selling substandard copper tubing to the Canadian public as the real thing.
Since then, in order to allow the substandard copper tubing to be used in British Columbia, the previous provincial government reduced the standard to 85 per cent of the recommended thickness.
I was amazed to learn that copper tubing, a major component in all plumbing installation, does not need to have the Canadian Standards Association's stamp of approval even though all plumbing and electrical fixtures used in Canada require the CSA approval.
I would strongly urge that the federal government work with the provinces to insist on CSA approval for all copper tubing sold in Canada to protect Canadian consumers from being misled by companies such as Wolverine Tube and to ensure that products are provided as specified.
Canadians should not tolerate inferior products to be sold as quality products at non-competitive prices.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, yesterday this government announced a $95 million charade called the Northern Ontario Development Agreement.
While this government was announcing it in as many cities and as often as it could, it forgot to mention one small detail. The agreement represents a cut of over 50 per cent for northern Ontario.
According to the government, this package was designed to help in the areas of forestry, mining and tourism with an injection of $95 million. However, prior to this agreement combined funding in these same areas amounted to over $220 million.
Let us look at what this government has done for northern Ontario. It gave us high interest rates and high dollar policies which all but wiped out our exporting resource industries. It gave us a 15 per cent softwood lumber surtax. It cancelled mineral exploration incentive programs. It cancelled our train service and our
November 5, 1991

flights. It cut research and development, native education and the Small Craft Harbours Program. Of course, it gave our tourism industry a 7 per cent go-south tax.
Now, it has kicked an economy that is already down by cutting funding by over 50 per cent. Why does it seem that the government's on-again, off-again deficit fight is always on when it comes to northern Ontario?
For the people of northern Ontario, it is clear that competitiveness and this government do not go hand in hand.

speakerposition: subtopic

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on Saturday, the French ambassador to Canada, Mr. Francois Bujon de l'Estang, left this country after a posting of more than two years. The ambassador told a reporter from Le Droit what his feelings were upon leaving this country, and I quote: "I leave with very positive feelings about a friendly country with tremendous potential. But I am surprised to see Canadians wallow in pessimism and self-pity, without realizing how lucky they are". The ambassador went on to say: "Canada is a rich country; it has plenty of space, a wealth of natural resources, an abundance of cheap energy, a determined and tolerant people and solid democratic traditions. Canada is a kinder, less harsh and more tolerant America".
In a nutshell, the ambassador told us we have a country that complains without realizing how lucky it is.

Mr. Speaker, last Friday, Chief Bernard Ominayak and Indian Affairs Minister Tom Siddon met face to face. It was the first high level meeting since the government attempted to ram its destructive take it or leave it offer down the throats of the Lubicon Indian nation nearly three years ago.
On Sunday, Alberta Solicitor General Dick Fowler indicated that the provincial government would stand by the Grimshaw Accord reached in October 1988. All that now stands in the way of a final settlement of this outstanding national disgrace is the federal government's continuing refusal to negotiate adequate economic development provisions and compensation for decades of abuse and assault inflicted upon the Lubicon people by successive Canadian governments.
It is the federal government that must act now to reopen unconditional negotiations and make the first move toward the achievement of a just and liveable settlement for the people of the Lubicon Indian nation.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the federal government proposes to increase Canadians' rights by putting the right to own property in the Constitution. Last week, a number of groups met in Ottawa to discuss this and agreed on this statement:
We believe that everyone should have the right to ownership and enjoyment of property, and not to be deprived thereof except by due process and with just compensation.
We believe this right should be given equal weight with the other rights the Charter protects.
We acknowledge that this right to property is subject to, and restricted by, such reasonable limits prescribed by government through law as can be justified in a fair and democratic society.
Given the above, we seek to have property rights included in the Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms.
Among the groups who signed this are the P.E.I. Property Owners' Association, Canadian Real Estate Association, Taxpayers' Coalition of Ontario, Alberta Real Estate Association, Fraser Institute, Fair Rental Policy Organization of Ontario, Canadian Homebuilders Association, Ontario Real Estate Association, Toronto Real Estate Board, and the Canadian Condominium Institute.
These organizations support the government's proposal to give Canadians more constitutionally guaranteed rights.

Mr. Speaker, to design the public exhibit base celebrating CBC's history as an integral part of the national fabric of Canada, to highlight its use of technology, its management decided to hire an American business whose interpretation will greet us at the front door. To me, it is the ultimate insult to Canadian creators.
Why did Canada's premier cultural institution take this decision? CBC says it was because the foreigners best understood their role in Canadian life. After the poetic cries of support for the CBC, I for one do not think it had to leave Canada to find creators who understand the CBC's role in our lives.
It is easy to suggest that opposition to Americans interpreting Canadian culture is xenophobic, but that would be to miss the point. What we have here is a publicly supported cultural institution whose mandate says it should be predominantly and distinctively Canadian and contribute to the shared national identity. Is it not then contradictory for the CBC to turn to foreigners for self-interpretation?
Let us hope in the future that national cultural institutions will engage Canadian creators and not engage in cross-border shopping.

Certainly the system is abused by some people, but what about a radiologist who can earn up to $600,000 a year? it would be better to re-evaluate our services, some of which are underused.B

One example is the double standard which allows consumers to take advantage of preferred tariff treatment with the U.S., with virtually no paperwork when importing goods from the U.S. as long as there is some indication that the item was manufactured in the United States.
However, if a Canadian business imports the same item for resale under the same tariff treatment, the business must obtain from the manufacturer cumbersome documentation which often makes it impractical

November 5, 1991
Oral Questions
for the business and in many cases the information is just simply not available, which then obviously makes it impossible.
As a result, Canadian business is prevented from offering to the Canadian consumer the same merchandise as the U.S. business at competitive prices.

Mr. Speaker, my question is for the Minister responsible for Constitutional Affairs. I was told that he would be in the House, but since he is not I will put my question to the

The government accepted this proposal in the Speech from the Throne, on May 13. However, we know that the committee started work late in September and today, in early November, we realize that it is not working well. speakerposition: Prime Minister
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, yes, the parliamentary committee has some problems.
It's a circus.

speakerposition: Prime Minister
speechtext: Well, the two independents in the House say that it is a circus. It is an honest attempt by the three main parties in this House to take part in drawing up a new constitution. And when you involve 30 or 35 people in a process across a country as vast as Canada, there are start-up problems. That being said, I am told that Senator Castonguay and Mrs. Dobbie have taken certain measures to greatly improve the effectiveness of the committee. If so, and we shall monitor it closely, although a joint committee of Parliament is to be independent, we shall keep a watchful eye on it and if we see shortcomings we shall extend the co-operation not only of the government but of Parliament as a whole, because it is an important national commission working in the national interest.

November 5, 1991

to see that this job is done in the interest of Canadians as quickly as possible.

Mr. Speaker, I share the concern expressed by my hon. friend and I think all members of the House do, with the exception of a few freeloaders over here who like to take advantage of Canadian unity while they are trying to undermine it.
It was pleasant last week to find out the latest proposal about an independent Quebec. You could have an independent Quebec, as described by their leader, Mr. Parizeau. They were going to have an independent Quebec with Canadian money, with a Canadian economic union and now with Canadian citizenship and a Canadian passport. Why would you go to all the trouble? The minister has just arrived in the House and I know that he will want to assure the Leader of the Opposition personally of his interest in this matter and his desire to work very closely with the co-chairs to ensure a greater degree of effectiveness so that as many Canadians as possible can be heard in what is an important contribution to nation-building.

Mr. Speaker, the Canadian Federation of Independent Business today released a report which states that the GST has had a devastating impact on Canadian small business.
I would like to ask the Minister of Finance if he concurs with the results reported in this study or does he have any facts, not theories but facts, which contradict the report?

speakeroldname: Hon. Otto Jelinek (Minister of National Revenue):
speakerposition: Minister of National Revenue
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, we have always recognized that there would be difficulties with a major tax change of this nature and we said it well prior to implementation.
However, we do not agree with Mr. Bulloch's conclusions in any way, shape or form because the study as announced today by Mr. Bulloch is incomplete, if not flawed. It overlooks some very, very serious points. For example, it did not include the administrative costs of the federal sales tax which businesses paid for while it was there, and the 22,000 exemptions and loopholes which we scrapped for the benefit of the business community.

November 5, 1991
Oral Questions
It did not include transitional tax credit or the accelerated write-offs and so on. Most of all, it overlooked the fact that most of the financial costs are either recoverable or deductible as business expenses.
This government said in advance of the implementation of the GST, after we scrapped the outgoing federal manufacturers' sales tax, that we would continue to consult with business and with Canadians as a whole to try to improve and simplify the system whenever and wherever possible. The Minister of Finance is going to be announcing some adjustments later this afternoon.
I invite Mr. Bulloch to come and work with us on behalf of business, instead of against us. That is not constructive.

Mr. Speaker, this is not an issue of implementing the tax, this is an issue of tax policy and the Minister of Finance should be answering for it.
Last week the government made the display of wanting to go out and consult with the public on the issue of competitiveness. If the minister is unwilling to accept the CFIB's findings on the impact of this tax, is he prepared to undertake immediately a public review and consultation study of the impact of the GST on Canadian business?

speakeroldname: Hon. Otto Jelinek (Minister of National Revenue):
speakerposition: Minister of National Revenue
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, there are two very important factors that the hon. member forgets.
The first factor is that studies, royal commissions, including an all-party parliamentary committee, agreed categorically and unanimously for the last 40 years that the federal manufacturers' sales tax had to be scrapped and replaced with something fairer and more modern like a value added tax which is being successfully used in some 48 other countries.
The other factor that the hon. member forgets is that there was a consultative process leading up to the implementation of the GST. There were some 6,000 business seminars. There were some 135,000 visits with business people to help them prepare. Virtually all business organizations-and I have to specifically compliment the Retail Council of Canada-worked in support of their membership to prepare them for the adjustments, except for the CFIB, and I would hope that the CFIB would once and for all start working on behalf of business instead of against them.

speakerposition: N.D.P. House Leader
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my question is directed to the Minister of Finance.
All Canadians appreciate the value of the small business sector in terms of driving the economy, particularly in the future, and job creation in the country. In the government's own goods and services tax information booklet for small business, it said that the GST would lower operating costs. The CFIB today indicated that the average cost for business is in excess of $9,000. It also said it would improve cash flow. We know that the GST has massacred small business. Some 13,000 have gone bankrupt in this past year. Another 20,000 have had to walk away from their businesses.
My question to the Minister of Finance is this. Knowing the reality of the GST, why did the government mislead Canadian small business about the effects of the GST?

speakeroldname: Hon. Otto Jelinek (Minister of National Revenue):
speakerposition: Minister of National Revenue
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the New Democrats have constantly been blaming the free trade agreement for lost jobs and they were wrong in trying to blame the free trade agreement. Now they are trying to blame the GST for lost jobs and they are just as wrong in trying to blame the GST.
I repeat what I said in reply to the earlier question, that the methodology used by Mr. Bulloch in the study is flawed. It does not'include many of the elements, including the discounting of nearly $1 billion of start-up costs for small businesses, or the $2.3 billion of GST credits to low and modest income Canadians. The fact of the matter is that all royal commissions over the years have categorically concluded that the federal manufacturers' sales tax must be scrapped and replaced with a value-added tax in order to make Canadian businesses more competitive. Can the hon. member not get that into his head, that the federal manufacturers' sales tax taxed the cost of doing business. The GST does not.

speakerposition: N.D.P. House Leader
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I want to suggest to the hon. minister that it was not the New Democratic Party, it was Catherine Swift of the CFIB who this morning estimated that between 100,000 and
200,000	jobs were lost because of the GST alone.
My question goes back to the Minister of Finance who knows full well the Gallup polls indicate that in excess of 70 per cent of Canadians are against the GST. This morning we find out that 70 per cent of the small business community across Canada is also against the

GST. I want to say very categorically that the New Democratic Party is also against the GST, 100 per cent.
My question is for the Minister of Finance who has indicated an interest in consultation with Canadians. Some 70 per cent of Canadians say it is wrong and 70 per cent of the small business sector say it is wrong. I suspect that Main Street, Vegreville says it is wrong. Will the minister now say that 70 per cent of Canadians are wrong in their GST opposition?

speakeroldname: Hon. Otto Jelinek (Minister of National Revenue):
speakerposition: Minister of National Revenue
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the hon. member wants to scrap the GST. How would he replace the revenues? He wants to scrap the free trade agreement. How would he open up markets to the business community of the country?
The member quoted some studies. I will quote another study which was recently done, granted in the Atlantic region only. It was done by an independent organization and concluded as follows: 80 per cent of small businesses feel that they understand the GST as it relates to their business; 77 per cent had no problem understanding and completing their forms; 94 per cent felt the service they received from Revenue Canada was helpful and courteous; and 92 per cent were satisfied with the over-all level of service offered by Revenue Canada.
It is quite obvious that Canadians are going to be concerned when a hidden tax is replaced by a fairer and open sales tax. But there is no doubt in any of those reports and royal commissions done during the last 40 years, including an all-party parliamentary committee which suggested that this government do the right thing for Canada, and that is exactly what this government has done.

speakerposition: N.D.P. House Leader
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I think it is clear to say that 70 per cent of Canadians and 70 per cent of the small business sector say they do not want a Tory GST or a Liberal GST. They want no GST, plain and clear.
I want to go back to the Minister of Finance who is going to ignore 70 per cent of the Canadian public, particularly 70 per cent of the small business sector. If the government is going to go ahead with this massacring type of tax, will he at least acknowledge that every small businessman and woman across the country has
Oral Questions
been turned into a federal tax collector, with absolutely no compensation? If the government is going to go ahead with this very punitive tax, at least compensate those who are collecting the tax for you.

speakeroldname: Hon. Otto Jelinek (Minister of National Revenue):
speakerposition: Minister of National Revenue
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, as the hon. member knows there is a compensation or subsidy to small business for the start-up costs.
The hon. member also quotes what the Canadian business and public want. They want greater productivity. They want greater job creation opportunities. The two things that are going to drive it there are lower interest rates, which are as low as they have been since 1978, and lower inflation rates which are lower today than they have been in the last 20 years.
That is the progress that this government has been making, and that is what the hon. member and John Bulloch should be applauding this government for.

Mr. Speaker, this government has been very concerned, as it should be, with Canada's declining competitiveness. As a matter of fact a year ago the then Minister of Finance told Canadians through this House that the GST was going to put Canadian business on a level playing field. Now 70 per cent of small business disagree with this tax. They say they have been hurt by it.
This is not an implementation problem. This is a fundamental policy problem. Will the Minister for Finance respond? He has not put Canadian business, at least small business, on a level playing field. He has thrown them into the showers. Won't he reconsider this tax measure?

Mr. Speaker, I am sure the hon. member is aware that the small business sector in Canada has the lowest corporate tax rate of any small business sector in the world. That recognizes the importance of small business to Canada.
He should also realize, and I know that he does, that under the federal sales tax it did hurt competition for Canadian concerns relative to those who were importing similar goods because the imports were taxed at roughly one-third that of comparable goods. He should also be aware that the over-all impact of the GST which is

November 5, 1991

refunded for business people has reduced the cost of capital by about 4 per cent.
All in all the application of the GST as a replacement for the FST has over all reduced the cost of doing business in Canada. That makes Canadian business more competitive.

Mr. Speaker, it is extraordinary that this minister could tell us that this tax has enhanced the competitiveness of Canadian small business, particularly small manufacturers. A majority of small manufacturers disagrees with the minister and says that this tax is worse than what we had before.
How can Canadians have faith in this government's ability to lead us into prosperity when its GST, according to all these studies, is working against small business?

speakeroldname: Hon. Don Mazankowski (Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of Finance):
speakerposition: Deputy Prime Minister; Minister of Finance; Vice-President
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the hon. member is a very intelligent member and understands business very well. He knows that what has occurred here is that when we brought in the GST we removed the 13.5 per cent federal sales tax which was a burden on business. It was recommended by royal commission after royal commission, parliamentary study after parliamentary study, that it should be scrapped for over six years.
This government had the courage to scrap it and in so doing has in fact improved the competitiveness of Canadian business.
I want to say something else. We know as well that the replacement of the FST with the GST has saved the farmers of Canada over a quarter of a billion dollars.

Mr. Speaker, my question is for the Minister of Finance.
The verdict is in. The GST has sucked nearly $10 billion from the bottom line of small businesses across Canada. It has caused a recession and cost over 100,000 Canadian jobs.
My question is: Will the government now admit what all Canadians already knew, that the GST was the wrong tax at the wrong time?

used in that study is absolutely false. It did not include many important elements in the conclusions of that study.
Another part is that the elimination of the federal manufacturers' sales tax, just to carry on from what the Minister of Finance said, is going to release over the next months and into next year as we come out of the recession some $9 billion of new economic activity.
That is probably the reason why the Leader of the Opposition now says he is going to keep the GST.

Mr. Speaker, my supplementary question is for the Minister of Finance.
Today the CFIB said, and I quote: "There is absolutely no justification, economic or political, for continuing to impose this costly, inefficient, regressive and unfair tax, the GST".
Will the government now take the advice of the CFIB and withdraw this badly flawed, unfair, inefficient and regressive tax, the GST? Yes or no.

speakeroldname: Hon. Otto Jelinek (Minister of National Revenue):
speakerposition: Minister of National Revenue
speechtext:

One of the elements in this report that we agree with whole-heartedly is harmonization of the GST with provincial sales taxes. We do not believe for a moment that objective of ours is dead. We are continuing as we stand here today discussing and consulting at the officials' level with the majority of provinces.
We would hope that the provinces will see the light of day and will see the benefits of harmonization not only for their businesses but their consumers as well. We continue to work toward that goal, that objective of having one tax, one system for Canada and Canadians.

Mr. Speaker, the minister as usual has brought out his excuse of harmonization as the answer to everything. In fact harmonization is going backward. Quebec has postponed it for six months. The province of Saskatchewan has backed out entirely. Will this government admit that the harmonization process is dead and recognize what the CFIB has therefore concluded, that it has to rethink entirely its sale tax project?

speakeroldname: Hon. Otto Jelinek (Minister of National Revenue):
speakerposition: Minister of National Revenue
speechtext:
No,
Mr. Speaker, we do not believe that the harmonization process is dead at all. We are not going to rethink our objective and goal of having one tax, one system.
I would hope that the hon. member would go to Queen's Park and talk to his friend and ours, the premier of Ontario, and ask him to rethink his position on harmonization because harmonization in Ontario, as in any other province, would help not only the business person and business in that province but certainly the consumer ultimately.

In fact, Mr. Speaker, the GST has damaged right across the province of Ontario, especially in border communities, small business, medium sized business, every form of business, and this minister knows it.

My supplementary question, Mr. Speaker, is as follows. Seventy per cent of Canadians are opposed to the GST. Why is the Minister of Finance not prepared to accept these recommendations and reconsider this proposal on the GST? Why is the minister not prepared to answer Canadians throughout this country?

Mr. Speaker, I am pleased today to speak on Bill C-17, which we have been studying for several months, originally as Bill C-80.
Motion No. 30, to delete lines 9 to 20, simply aims to avoid the renewal of firearms acquisition certificates. I ask that firearms acquisition certificates not be renewed, because renewals make it possible to avoid the 28-day period.
Also, the renewal would cost half as much as the original firearms acquisition certificate. Since the certificate would cost $50, renewing it would cost $25. People who buy firearms spend on average $500 and often more so they should not have us believe that $25 or $50 for a firearms certificate is too much.
Therefore, I believe that firearms users must pay for their sport, because hunting or target shooting is supposed to be a sport. I think users should pay for their sport.
The Legislative Committee on Bill C-17 heard many things. It heard people who came to testify, and I must say that many of these witnesses told us about the quality of life. I would simply like to mention a few associations that told us about quality of life. I will not give a complete list, but I must say that we got great support from the Canadian Association of Chiefs of Police, the Canadian Criminal Justice Association and the Federation of Canadian Municipalities. I have a very long list that it would be too tedious to read here, but I think it is important to tell the general public that we did get a lot of support.

November 5, 1991

Quite often, those who were opposed to any amendment and even to Bill C-17 itself were unfortunately Conservatives who basically did not support their minister.
Why did they act that way? They told us that it was because there is a very big difference between urban and rural ridings and that separate legislation was needed, which of course does not make any sense in law. In fact, the Canadian Bar Association told the Committee just that. Nevertheless, those arguments were made.
I now turn to my Motion No. 35. To make it easier to follow, I will show you. We heard all kinds of illogical and silly arguments, but in this motion, I simply ask that a photograph be attached to the firearms acquisition certificate. In fact, that is what we were promised, but unfortunately, this is what we have now from the Legislative Committee. The bill says-and I will tell you exactly what I want to change-that a firearms acquisition certificate must be in the form prescribed by the Commissioner and shall, unless the Commissioner deems otherwise, be accompanied by a photograph of the holder.
As an argument against this provision, we were told that there were people whose religion prohibited the taking of photographs. They cannot be photographed because of their religion. That is the argument that was used against that provision.

My colleague asks if drawings are all right. That might be a good suggestion to make. That is why I wanted to tell you that we received some rather strange proposals which, unfortunately, have led to the legislation before us.
It would be much simpler to specifically mention that religion, since its followers must certainly be proud to practise it. It would also be interesting to know how many people belong to that faith in Canada. We are not going to pass an act that supposedly applies to everybody
but in the end only applies to some exceptions, unless it is an indirect way of not having a photograph attached to the firearms acquisition certificate. I certainly hope that is not the case. The Firearms Control Coalition and others, asked for stricter control and the use of photographs as identification for buying a firearm or ammunition.
I proposed that amendment, which was rejected on the grounds that it was not in accordance with the spirit of the bill. According to the Chairman, it was out of order. They rejected the idea that firearms acquisition certificates be used when buying ammunition. If certificates are required for buying firearms, they should always bear a photograph, as we requested, since it is well known that people exchange certificates to buy firearms. That was the purpose of that motion.
Of course I do not think that we should criticize everything in the bill since it is a step in the right direction, but I must say that it is only a step.
A small step.

A small step indeed. We also asked that every firearm be registered. That procedure could have been implemented in the near future. We did not ask for registration of all the firearms that are presently in Canada. We asked that this registration process start at a future date, on January 1, 1993. This amendment was also rejected because apparently it went beyond the scope of the bill.
Unfortunately I think that we disappointed quite a few people that way. In our opinion, this is an important measure and it will have to be implemented eventually. This government will not do it. Unfortunately it is not the Conservative government that will do it. It will be another government that will take credit for it then. Too bad for those people; they will not be able to take advantage of the situation. The field is open right now. Everybody wants it.
They need something to their credit.

They sure do. That is what I am told here, but that is another matter. Maybe. In concluding, we would have liked more improvements to Bill C-17, but of course, we will have to content ourselves with what little we have now since, as I said, this is all that we were able to get.
November 5, 1991

Mr. Speaker, I thank my friend for yielding.
I rise to speak at the beginning of what I believe is an historic debate. This is on gun control. As members know, this is the second bill this year. We have had a lot of committee meetings in which all members have participated and we have had a lot of give and take in this House on this bill.
I know people see some things that go on in the House and on TV but behind the scenes there is a lot of work. Many members, including the one who just spoke, members of the Liberal Party and government members, have put a lot of effort into this bill.
The country is watching today because there is a lot of interest in this.

Mrs. Lapointe-Edwards is here. She lost her daughter in the massacre at the Ecole Polytechnique in Montreal.

She has shown great courage in following this bill through until today and so have other people. Everybody has good motives, I believe.
The New Democratic Party has tried to have one constant position throughout and it is that we are in favour of strong but effective gun control. We do not want a bureaucracy that will hurt genuine hunters, trappers, competition shooters and even collectors. But we do want effective gun control.
Canada is not the United States. This country was settled peacefully and it was settled without the use of guns. That is part of the Canadian culture and all members of this House and all Canadians share that.
Therefore we welcome the bill. I would just like to state briefly what the bill does.
Just to summarize what the bill does, it prohibits automatic weapons that have been converted to fire in a semi-automatic form. These guns have flowed into Canada in the last few years. There are about 50,000 of them in the country. Unfortunately they are grandfathered in this bill-that means people can keep them-and
Government Orders
we will discuss that later on. We have some amendments about that. But the fact is that these guns have no place in hunting or any legitimate purpose. They are military guns and the government is moving to prohibit them.
Second, the legislation prohibits or restricts semi-automatic military assault rifles. It is going to be done by regulation. It is not dependent on this bill and we will be waiting to see these regulations. We do not want to see the Rambo culture in Canada. These guns are increasingly being imported into Canada and we want to pursue this in the debate that is going to follow today.
Third, there is a prohibition on large capacity magazines. As I understand it, semi-automatic handguns will have a ten-shot limit and centre-fired semi-automatic rifles and shotguns will have a five-shot limit. We will be discussing this as we go along. I remind the members that the large capacity magazine that Marc Lepine used enabled him to kill more people and that might have been prevented.
Fourth, this bill also changes the firearms acquisition certificate screening process to improve the screening so we will know that people who get guns are legitimate gun owners, not crazies or criminals. So there will be an improvement of the screening process.
Fifth, there will be safe storage in the bill. We are going to try to define that and deal with it so that someone does not store a gun unsafely and his or her teenage kid in a fit of depression gets the gun and commits suicide. We had 1,100 cases like that in Canada last year.
We are going to have tougher penalties in this bill to try and deal with criminals who misuse firearms. I think all of us are in favour of that and we want to improve that.
Finally, there will be a parliamentary review of these regulations. We will get back to this.
This is a modest proposal. My first amendment deals with the matter of the firearms acquisition certificate. We have the technical ability and we have witnesses who came before the committee and asked why we do not now register guns on a firearms acquisition certificate. This could be done when people buy guns so we know where all future guns are and how many we have in the country. We could trace lost or stolen guns and so on. That is what we propose to do.

There has been an awful lot of opposition to that in the country and the government has not accepted that. It is not in this bill. That is why it is a modest bill.
But I say to the government, to other members, to hunters and people who have opposed this; let us look at the broader picture. It is not going to hurt legitimate firearm owners. We want to get at the illegitimate firearm owners and we want to have a strong bill. I hope that we will see a future bill that will include firearms acquisition certificates so that there is a form of registration of guns when they are bought. I hope the members will adopt my amendment. I am not holding my breath but I would like to see that in the bill.
I have outlined what is in the bill and why it is a modest proposal. I think it could have gone farther and I am going to introduce amendments today. It could have dealt with controlling ammunition and tougher criminal sanctions. It could have nailed down a bit more what the parliamentary scrutiny is on the bill. It could have dealt with getting regulations before the House. Most of this bill will be in the regulations. We would like to see the regulations before the House to see what is in the bill.
The government has set up a system wherein there will be control through regulations. It will be vetted by the Firearms Board Advisory Council and the House of Commons, so legitimate hunters need not worry.
I just want to end by saying that I believe Canadians are for gun control. I believe Canadians want strong gun control. They want effective gun control. They understand that this is part of Canadian culture, that this is a peaceful society. I believe events have shown that we need that. We want no more incidents of the Marc Lepine type. I know they are impossible to really prevent but gun control works.
It worked after the first bill in 1976.1 predict it is going to work after this bill and we should fight to further strengthen it.

Mr. Speaker, I want to follow on what the last member has said.
I think that everyone in this House in a responsible way supports the safe use of guns and the control of guns in society.
In our society today we have to be really tough if we are going to control it. It seems to me that it does not matter how well we make up legislation in this House, it is never going to be enough to do a very difficult task. But if we do not start somewhere we will not get anything done.
I want to say a word today on my amendment with regard to the cost of firearms acquisition certificates. Members who sat on the committee and in this House will know that this has been a big issue.
My main concern is the case of the farm community where there is an outbreak of rabies or predators such as wolves. The farmer may have to go out to buy a rifle for the first time in his life.
It is going to cost him $50, a figure that is being thrown around, although we know it is not cast in stone. That gun will be used on the property for the legitimate purposes of protecting animals and the health of people and other animals on the farm.
Here you have a legitimate reason for buying a gun. I guess my feeling is that I see people like that paying for the over-all program when actually they need it for their own particular way of life. They are legitimate arms owners and they are certainly going to be no problem to society.
Similarly, I had another amendment that was not accepted on the compensation for collectors of firearms who find out after the regulations come in that they have a firearm that is illegal. These firearms collectors have collected these items during times when it was legal for them to do so. Some have put out quite a lot of money for their collections.
They are going to have to give up those firearms without any compensation within a certain period of time. After that they will be in illegal possession of those firearms.
The reason behind my submission of that particular amendment was that I think there is a far greater chance of gun collectors declaring what they have in their collection if they are going to get some compensation for the weapons they have collected over the years.
There might be a tendency not to turn them in if they find out they are not going to get any compensation for

them whatsoever. That was the real intent behind the particular amendment that has not been accepted.
The amendment to Bill C-17 which I put down with regard to the cost of firearms acquisition certificates does specify the amount to be paid by applicants for the reasons which I have mentioned.
I felt it was unfair to charge people who need guns because of their way of life whether they are farmers, hunters, trappers or whatever.
They are honest citizens going in to purchase firearms acquisition certificates, whereas we will have other people of course who will not do it in that way. The criminal element is certainly not going to do it in a fair and open way.
At the present time Bill C-17 stipulates that the Crown will determine the cost of firearms acquisition certificates and renewals by regulation. The only requirement is that the firearms acquisition certificate renewals must be one-half the amount of the firearms acquisition certificate application fee.
The government has provided figures of $50 for firearms acquisition certificates and $25 for renewals, which is rather steep when they become a necessity. These figures are not set in stone and can be changed by the Governor in Council. The Governor in Council could virtually increase it beyond this amount for people who require firearms in the daily routine of their lives.
By amending clause 18 of the bill, the amount paid for firearms acquisition certificates will be specifically set at $17. The fee for firearms acquisition certificate renewals will be set at $10. If this amendment is adopted the Governor in Council will have to introduce legislation in order to change the amounts charged for firearms acquisition certificates and renewals.
This is to protect that group of people on whose behalf I have argued before who should not have to pay the full amount because guns are used in their way of life. I am thinking of the farming community today and farmers certainly do not have an abundance of cash. They are having a very difficult time out there and you do have times when rabies become very prominent in certain regions. Today there are problems out there with wolves attacking animals on farms. So it seems to me that we are adding an extra burden to people in a particular
Government Orders
occupation in this country where their overhead and costs are already extremely high.
Clause 19 of Bill C-17 authorizes the Governor in Council to issue firearms acquisition certificates to people who are under 18 years of age. This clause is perhaps included in the bill to address the concerns of the native community.
This proposed amendment to clause 19 specifies that the application fees for firearms acquisition certificates and the renewal thereof for this group of people, will be $17 and $10 respectively, rather than being subject to regulation. This proposed amendment to the bill provides uniformity in the fees for firearms acquisition certificates and renewals.
Therefore my representations today, as I have said, are really aimed at the people who may need a new firearm by necessity: farmers, hunters or other people who need them in their regular way of life.
I have no sympathy whatsoever, as nobody has in this House, for those who try to abuse the system by gathering up firearms without following the law of the firearms acquisition certificate.
We in Canada have always been very responsible in the way we have handled these issues. I want to compliment our critic for the fair way he has handled this bill in committee and others who brought forward the representations of people across this country. I think it has been a very open discussion on the part of all members of Parliament. Those of us who come from large rural ridings, and I include my colleagues from northern Ontario, may have somewhat different views on some of these issues but that is because of our backgrounds. speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I want to make some comments with respect to the seven motions that are before the House at the present time. Before doing so I want to agree with the member for Renfrew-Nipissing-Pembroke that this has been an open process. It has been a very productive process. There has been a great deal of consultation and study by parliamentarians on this bill. It has been amended a number of times since we first saw it in its

November 5, 1991
Government Orders
first incarnation as Bill C-80 and I think the bill before us is certainly a more effective bill.
The seven amendments that are here refer specifically to the firearms acquisition certificate. I do not want to let my comments trail off into other areas of the bill. I would be pleased to talk about them as they arise through the amendment process but we are dealing here with the firearms acquisition certificate.
When I first began meeting with individuals and sitting in on discussions that the Minister of Justice had with national groups from across this country everyone said the same thing. There are problems with the firearms acquisition certificate. That is the one thing people were unanimous on.
I remember one group pointing out to the then Minister of Justice, Mr. Lewis, that the form does not even provide for a change of address. Obviously that is a problem. I believe there was not enough of a security component within the firearms acquisition certificate process as well. I think there are problems with the fee schedule which was written in 1978 and was written right into the bill.
Parliament does not tackle these bills every year, and perhaps for good reason, but writing in an amount I think is a bad idea.
We have made a number of changes through the FAC and I think all of them improved the situation. One of them, as the hon. member for Saint-Hubert mentioned, is the requirement in the general case that photographs be required. She mentioned the fact that it is not an absolute requirement that every FAC have a photograph and she asked under what circumstances there would be exceptions. She mentioned at committee stage she heard there was one religious group who objects to photographs. For her information I believe it is the Flutterites.
There was another reason we did not make it absolute in the bill. It may be very difficult particularly in the northern section of Canada. Camera equipment may not be readily available and it may be a situation in Canada's far north where the hunter or the individual would be well enough known that there would be no question as to that person's identity.
It was for those reasons that there was not the absolute requirement but we would expect that in 99-point-something percentage of the cases we would have photographs, and it is a good idea. I do not think individuals who have it will mind because it protects them as well in case their firearms acquisition certificate is stolen.
These amendments are coming from two different areas. The hon. member for Saint-Hubert asked why there was a reduction in the fees upon renewal. She questioned the whole renewal process in one of her amendments.
The member from the Liberal Party who just spoke questioned why the fee was set at $50. As I indicated at the committee, $50 is what the Government of Canada believes is its cost in administering this program. We try to operate a number of these things on a cost recovery basis to the extent possible. It is our belief that $50 will pay for the system.
As good a Conservative as I am, I certainly agree with efforts by the government to try and balance its books on as many programs as possible.
I should indicate to hon. members that the cost of the registration of restricted weapons which is also part of the firearms regime, although not specifically addressed in these amendments or the bill, is borne by the Canadian taxpayer. The cost of registering restricted weapons comes out of general revenue.
The firearms acquisition certificates are on a cost recovery basis. It is our belief that it is about $50. A number of colleagues at committee said: "Look, we want to keep people within the system. We want to provide an incentive for those who have an FAC to renew it". There is no requirement that a person renew their FAC. However if we waive the waiting period for those individuals who do have a valid FAC and are renewing theirs and charge a reduced fee we encourage people to stay within the system. We think that is a a good idea and the committee adopted that as well.
My hon. friend in the New Democratic Party from Port Moody-Coquitlam asked: "Why not tag in a registration system?" I do not want to accept an amendment that puts in a registration system without having everything that might go with it if that is the direction we want to go in.
November 5, 1991

The amendment he has would only require the local firearms officer to register the firearm. I am not quite sure what that would give us. I do not see any requirement there for a person moving to another jurisdiction. There is no central retrieving system and no provision here to pay for that kind of a system.
Just because this might ultimately make sense to some members I do not want to tag in an amendment here. It would require an enormous administrative task for very little gain if this was hooked into some national system, but that is not what the amendment says. I think there would have to be a lot more thought given to it. The firearms acquisition certificate would be changed to something different. It is not a possession certificate, it is an acquisition certificate.
We could argue whether a person should have a valid FAC just to possess a firearm. We could argue about that for the rest of the afternoon but that is not the regime that was set up in 1978 and is not part of the regime which we have modified at the present time.
That in sum is where we are going with the FAC. I think it is a dramatic improvement. There is one comment that the hon. member for Renfrew-Nipissing- Pembroke made that I want to draw to the attention of the House.
He mentioned the case of the individual who may not be able to afford the $50 and what about him? Although it is not in Bill C-17 it continues to be part of the law of Canada. The Criminal Code states, and I will read the section: "That no fee is payable in respect of a firearms acquisition Certificate that is issued to a person who requires a firearm to hunt or trap in order to sustain himself or his family".
That is the wording in that section. There is provision for exemption for those individuals who hunt for a living. I would not want to leave an impression that there was no provision. It is a reasonable package.
I know I only have one minute. Section 2 which I do support is a technical amendment by the government which tightens up the description of an FAC and eliminates one of the definitions of an FAC that has not been of use or of benefit to us in the past 12 years.
I am urging hon. members to accept Motion No. 2 and to reject the other six that are proposed at this time.
