speakeroldname: Mr. Rob Nicholson (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I suppose that of all the amendments we might have the least amount of debate on these. These are technical amendments to assure that the French and English versions of the bills are as exact as possible. Many of them were recommended by Mr. Claude Ryan, the Quebec minister responsible for this area, and the technical analysis of the bill recommended a number of these changes.
We strive as always to have the bills conform in both official languages so that they both say the same thing, and these amendments accomplish that.

Mr. Speaker, unfortunately what we have here is just a few technical amendments proposed by the minister. We had hoped the minister would do better than that.
We are well aware-and this was clear from the proceedings of the legislative committee, and especially the actions of the government's chief Whip, which were in fact criticized by one of the members-that the
Government Orders
majority has unfortunately left the Minister of Justice very little leeway.
Sometimes we get the impression that the Prime Minister would rather travel abroad and talk about disarmament and human rights instead of supporting his Minister of Justice within his own party, to meet the minimum demands of those Canadians who are anxious about public health and support genuine gun control.
The process has shown how a very broad consensus evolved in Canadian and Quebec society, not only among the people directly concerned but also, for instance, among all public health authorities in Quebec, who intervened on numerous occasions before the committee, first before the special committee and later before the legislative committee. Every time, the bill was improved a little more.
After the hearings of the Special Committee, there was an improvement, assessed at about 10 per cent of what people were asking. On the legislative committee some elements were further clarified, but we obviously have a long way to go, because the technical amendments now before the House contain no reference at all to the public health problem. This bill is still essentially based on the concept that we have the right to possess arms and that our freedom should be restricted as little as possible, and I am referring especially to the desire for minimal controls on people who possess arms in a civilized society.
Why object to the registration of all firearms? This would be a way to find out how many firearms there are in Canada. At the present time, no one knows how many firearms we have in this country. This would help us find out who the owners are.
Is it too much to ask, Mr. Speaker, considering that not only most unfortunate and painful incidents are caused by some deranged people but also that often guns are known to be used to commit suicide.
Quebec health care officials spoke at length of this issue before the committee. Yet, nothing in this bill would make it possible to initiate an education process to focus on the fact that it is a privilege to own a gun and that in a civilized society such a privilege is to be exercised with some restraint.

November 5, 1991
Government Orders
I just cannot understand why the minister was unable to convince her caucus of this obvious fact, especially after the whole process the committee has gone through.
There have been some improvements, for instance in the definition of the genuine gun collector, and I think that, in that respect, it is going in the right direction.
But another fundamental aspect of this bill has gone unchanged: it promises a number of things that can only come through when regulations are made, which means going to an advisory committee which, I am told, is made up for the most part of people who consider guns as very important.
So, we will have to wait for the regulations to know if the minimum set in this bill will indeed be reflected in them and implemented by the government. It is this second aspect of the bill that makes us somewhat sceptical. Basically, the provisions of this bill are telling us that, yes, we are taking a step forward, but in order to see if this step was indeed taken you will have to wait for the government regulations.
In this respect, one particular part is most unfortunate, the part dealing with prohibited firearms. We will still have to decide if such and such a firearm is prohibited, when based on technological advances and all that we could have really protected the public. Instead, we will have to wait for more unfortunate incidents to happen before designating a particular type of firearm as prohibited.
A much simpler and more normal way to go, as in the case of drugs and various hazardous goods, would have been to start by controlling the sale of firearms and ammunition. Then, it would have been possible to allow only those deemed to meet the legal criteria to be sold, instead of acting after the fact. EIow many of these firearms will have been sold by then?
It is especially important in the Canadian context, because of our proximity to the United States where arms are in wide circulation. We are asking our customs officers at the border to determine whether or not a weapon is prohibited. We are in fact asking them to become weapons experts on top of everything. Customs officers came to testify before our committee. They said: "We already have trouble controlling. The controls must be made much simpler". It would have been very easy to
say: "Here are the allowed weapons and all those that are not on the allowed list cannot be imported. If you want to import them or sell them in Canada or Quebec, you will first have to obtain permission and know for sure that this weapon satisfies criteria acceptable under the law".
Now we will intervene after the fact; we will act when unfortunate incidents occur and public opinion demands that we take another step forward. The minister told us that she expected it to happen in future, but that the attitudes of our MPs. Unfortunately it holds true for many members on this side of the House. We will see other amendments that were proposed to further diminish the bill as presented.
I think that despite the minister's efforts, it is very clear to us that she was unable to assert leadership and have the support of her Prime Minister and Cabinet colleagues to convince the members of her caucus to go further and come up with a minimum acceptable to everyone who is concerned with public health and protection.
I am convinced that most hunters, who in order to have the right to exercise their hunting privilege accept far greater restrictions than registering their weapons, would have quite willingly accepted being required just to register their weapon.

speakerposition: Bloc Québécois House Leader
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I must say something about these insignificant amendments proposed by the minister. My colleague from Rosemont, and particularly the hon. member for Saint-Hubert, have both examined this bill in detail and they spent many hours listening to different groups across Canada, especially from Quebec. I want to congratulate them because their convictions did not change when they changed affiliation. I know that these members, who were extremely active when they were in the Conservative caucus, have done everything to convince the government to take stronger measures. Today again, they continue to defend those who believe in stricter control of firearms.
It is obvious that a superpowerful lobby has neutralized many of our colleagues who claim that they support public safety, that they sympathize with the unfortunate victims and their families, but who will only make a very timid effort to push for limited gun control. Unfortunately we are in a situation where a small step is better
November 5, 1991

than nothing at all, and even though we have strong reservations about this bill as a whole and think it does not go far enough, we are convinced that other amendments will have to be made very soon. After each incident, we will rise in this House to demand more amendments, and each time, the government will be on the defensive and will lengthen the list of prohibited weapons.
In fact, the reactive approach of the government makes it look as though we are trying to pull teeth. The government never fails to put itself in an impossible situation. I do not at all understand how the minister goes about her duties as Minister of Justice. Instead of following a pure, simple and clear principle to the effect that all firearms be registered, and then make exceptions, she takes the opposite approach and that explains the reluctance of the government to do anything in that field.
I would hope that this is not the result of the American influence. I would hope that they will not claim that the urban and rural realities are so different as to justify being so cautious with each detail of the bill, especially so as not to displease superpowerful lobbies.
As far as I know, the value of life is the same, whether one lives in the country or in the city. The same emotions are stirred and the same troubles ensue when firearms are misused in the city or in the country. A bullet is as deadly in the city as it is in the country.
When I hear this so-called lobby claim that it speaks on behalf of rural Canada, I am sorry but I think the problem is being misplaced. It is because the government is trying so hard not to displease anybody that we get this kind of legislation, a bill that lacks firmness and which essentially takes a backward approach. This is obvious to everyone. Almost 80 per cent of Canadians expected far stricter legislation. People respect athletes but respect law and order even more and do not want violence across this country.
Recently I was listening to a report on various gangs in Montreal who said that they used to settle their scores with their fists. It was not very civilized, but it was not as
Government Orders
bad as a gunshot. In fact, the leaders of these communities and these gangs said that now it was a lot more effective. Once they settled their scores, they stayed settled.
This legislation has no backbone. It will do nothing about the problems caused by various criminal acts. I think it is sad for all those people who spent so much time and energy during the past two years, struggling to make the government understand that we wanted to live in a society that was as peaceful as we could make it, that we wanted to ensure that firearms did not lie around in the back of the trunk of just about anybody's car at any time.
We wanted to ensure our children would be safe at night. We wanted to give life and ourselves the best possible break. But today we have a bill that tries to give people the best possible opportunity to possess arms. We think this is unacceptable, but like all Canadians we have to consider: What do we do? We have a government that has no guts. It is willing to move a little, no more. Then we have a choice: Do we vote against this bill? If the bill is defeated, all we have left is the law of the jungle, more or less.
So we are all in a difficult position as parliamentarians. We feel they lacked the courage of their convictions, that they lacked principle, but at the same time we are stuck with voting in favour of the bill, because a bird in the hand is worth two in the bush. We are really stuck. What worries us is that the government will probably use our support during the final vote on this bill to claim there was a general consensus in the House. There is no such thing. Unfortunately we are all more or less being held hostage, like the rest of Canadians. I want to pay tribute to all those people who did everything they could to try and convince the government to do more.
Earlier the hon. member for Saint-Hubert mentioned several groups. We all had visits from people of principle who wanted to tell us about some of their tragic experiences, often as a result of improper use of firearms. As parliamentarians we all had a chance to see how earnestly these men and women become involved in the parliamentary process, as every good citizen should.

Mr. Speaker, I would like to say a few words on this group of amendments. I heard the speech by the hon. member for Shefford, Quebec and I agree with some of what he just said, but not all. I am in the same position as he is.

situation. I say to members from Quebec that we must continue to insist on having more amendments accepted and other changes made in another bill, perhaps.
As I said in my first speech, much of this bill is already in the regulations. I think that we can do it and, as I said, I agree with the hon. member who spoke. I am in the same situation. We can see that it is not a very good bill, but it is acceptable. That is why we will vote for this bill.

Mr. Speaker, in the short time that I have, I would like to start my comments about the particular amendments that I have as they relate to clip size, magazine size, by prefacing my comments. I want to preface my comments very carefully because I understand the emotion that has been created in this debate. I want to try and focus on this legislation based on my knowledge of gun control and guns themselves and also based on my experience on the special committee. I want to focus on that because I think it is very important for people to keep in mind the long road that we have been down in the last few months.
I want to start off by suggesting to the members of the House and, indeed, to the public at large that unfortunately this piece of legislation has the complete wrong focus. I know all members in this place and the public out there really would like to see a stronger gun legislation. I am one of those who would prefer that we have better legislation as it relates to gun control in this country. Unfortunately, the government has done an excellent job of convincing all Canadians that this particular piece of legislation is going to make our streets safer, it is going to reduce crime and it is also going to somehow reduce homicides and accidents that are created by the use of firearms.
I want to relate to a national Gallup poll that was put out in September 1991. The wrong focus the government has taken is borne out in this particular poll.
Let me start off by reading this poll and then get into more specific details of the legislation.
No. 1 on the Gallup poll: Canadians were asked to pick the one thing in the following five choices whereby the government should mainly address the new gun control laws. The results were as follows: guaranteeing severe penalties for any crimes involving guns, 33 per cent; tighter screening of new gun buyers, 29 per cent; further limiting the types of guns that can be bought, 15 per cent; increasing the requirements in safety training, gun use and storage, 12 per cent; increasing restrictions over present gun owners, 8 percent.
Canadians agreed that the courts are presently much too lenient in punishing criminals using guns.

November 5, 1991
That was agreed to by 86 per cent of Canadians. The new law should control criminals and not guns by giving out much tougher penalties to those who use a gun in any crime. Again 88 per cent were in favour of that.
Law abiding sportsmen, recreational shooters and collectors should not lose their guns because of the actions of relatively few criminals. Again 82 per cent of Canadians agreed with that statement.
Passing more severe laws over legitimate gun owners will have very little influence on criminals, and 69 per cent of Canadians agreed with that. I do not feel well informed about the issues related to gun control because I have not been given clear or complete information about the subject, and 50 per cent of Canadians agree with that.

speechtext:
That in the opinion of this House the government should consider bringing its defence policy out into the open so that there can be a full public debate on the over-all logic of our defence position.
He said: Mr. Speaker, I suppose as I stand to speak on this private members' motion, those who watch the cameras and perhaps some of our colleagues on all sides of the House would say:"Why is he speaking and on which subject is he speaking?"
I think this is a very important subject and this is why raised it in my resolution. It may not be related to my immediate riding problem, which is basically a problem of the failure of the fishery, but the subject of defence is very pertinent and very close to the hearts of Newfound-
Private Members' Business
landers, and I am sure to all Canadians, for a number of reasons.
I know the time I have and I want to say to members on all sides of the House, that this can be a partisan issue. I do not want it to be a partisan issue. The motion, very simply stated, says that we would like to see a larger debate on national defence. If I quote government sources, if I quote the sources on my side of the House, it is only to make the point that there should be a longer discussion on this subject.
I would indulge you, Mr. Speaker, if I become partisan perhaps you could remind me because I do not intend to, but should I, I suppose I could be forgiven for this.
Sir John Hackett, who was a great writer about military things, said: "What a country gets from the military is what it asks for, nothing more, and nothing less. And when it looks into the hearts and minds of those in uniform, those men and women in uniform, what it sees is a reflection of itself. And if the mirror is a true one, the reflection will be as accurate as the mirror is".
When I was in uniform I was always impressed by that because I knew that in this House was a great concern about our military people. I did not design the timing but I think it should not go without notice that it is very close to November 11. Activities that have taken place in the last few days reflect how important the military is in our lives.
By way of putting things in perspective, I want to read the opening statement of the old defence paper. I say the old defence paper, but it is the last one we have had, really. This is not meant to be partisan and I just want to put it in perspective because it could have been the Prime Minister of any party who said this.
If I had been a prime minister or if it had been my party I think I would have said that as well. It is not meant to be partisan. Prime Minister Mulroney said: "No government has a more important obligation than to protect the life and the well-being of its people, to safeguard their values and interests, and in Canada it is a time to renew that commitment". That was the beginning.
I worked very closely with the white paper on defence and I suppose in some ways it would be difficult for me to stand up here and say that I disagreed with what was in there. I am certainly aware that the circumstances have

November 5, 1991
Private Members' Business
changed since that paper was put together. I want to read the conclusion of that paper:
"The government will implement this program vigorously. Over time our endeavours will produce a defence posture responsive to the challenges of 1990 and beyond. Canadian security and sovereignty will be better served. Canada will become a more responsible ally and we will have a firmer basis from which to contribute to peace and freedom."
As I said earlier, that could have been written by any government, it could have been written by any prime minister or any defence minister.
Since then there have been developments. In some ways I am almost embarrassed that this cannot be more partisan, but I would share the views of the government that it is very difficult to organize a defence policy when things are changing so rapidly.
I know that I am certainly supported by my colleagues on this side of the House, and I see members on the other side of the House nodding as well. I would like to see a more public debate on this very important issue.
I had some notes but they are scattered all over the place. I had a very starched and ironed speech but it does not seem to be the time for it. I feel more comfortable speaking about defence and the notion of involving the Canadian public in a more positive sense, in a more continuing sense. Let me explain why I feel this.
Each time the budget comes out there IS a change in national defence. There have been base closures, there have been changes in the NATO structure, and I have to be honest, there are few things that have come out in the statements with which I have been able to take real issue. I am the kind of person who if there is a subject that I want to take issue with, I will, and if there is one that perhaps I would have to force, I would just as soon not.
Let us look at the defence policy statement that was made by the minister on, I think it was September 17. What did he say in that? He basically said that things are going to be as they were before, except we are going to have some changes.
I have been involved in the last 15 years in trying to work out defence policies and there are basically three ways you can do it. You can start with what you have and take it up or take it down. That is called the incremental defence policy. You can start with what you have and totally rearrange it. That is called the new change. This is what the white paper in 1987 did; the "new change". Or you can start and do something called zero base. You start from zero and you work out why you have so many people in uniform, what it is they are doing, and why they are doing it.
I have been in consultation with some of my former colleagues and I would never want to embarrass them. They are not upset by the policy as it is today, which is, I suppose, an incremental policy. I have here in my hand the statement on defence policy by the Minister of National Defence and the government, and I will read the first paragraph. It says:
Canada, like any country, must maintain its defence policy
periodically because of the requirement to maintain efficiency, adapt
to changes in the international situation, and to take into account the
realities peculiar to the territory.
That is great stuff. It is wonderful stuff, but what does
it mean?
We are the second largest country in the world and I wonder sometimes if we recognize really where the threats are. It is because of the unusual nature of the threat that I believe my motion should be considered seriously.
The motion basically says that we should talk more about defence policy in Canada.
Mr. Speaker, I know where you come from and I know that you have been involved in defence issues, perhaps not as a constituency matter but I know that you certainly have been involved peripherally.
There are a number of reasons why the 295 politicians in this House become involved in defence issues. Most of the time perhaps it is for the wrong reason. Perhaps a base is going to be closed or somebody is doing something and a politician has to go and make their number in the House of Commons.
If we were really to get down to basics, we would have to look at defence policy as an insurance policy. In the bad old days when there were wars and enemies on the other side of wherever, it was a fairly simple thing to say
November 5, 1991

that there was an enemy, we can afford this much for defence, and this is how much it is going to cost the taxpayer to protect against the enemy. Certainly in my lifetime that was reasonably clear. I knew more or less where the enemy was, or at least the perceived enemy in peacetime.
It was judgmental on the country as to how much money it would spend on defence.
There has been a transition in the last two years and a number of things have changed. How can you possibly say there is the enemy and this is how much we are going to spend? The government has a real problem. Anybody in government would have a problem in deciding how much to spend on national defence.
I think there are 166 or 167 countries in the United Nations today but in those days there were a lot fewer. The civilized world is a civilized organization very much like the way we run this House of Commons; we are civilized people, there is a Speaker, and we have certain rules that we are subjected to. We do not always follow them but we are subjected to them.
In 1945 the war ended. All of a sudden there was no enemy. The enemy of yesterday was the friend of tomorrow. In 1949 we started on NATO and we got NATO organized in 1950. Then things became lined. You knew you were on this side and you were a member of NATO. People joined NATO and then there was the other side, the Warsaw Pact. I would not say it was simple but I would say it was relatively clear about how you would line up.
Eighteen months ago that changed tremendously. Who is the enemy today? Where is the enemy? How is the enemy going to perform?
I would suggest that the enemy of today is more malicious than the enemy of yesterday. If I know my enemies, I may not be happy with them but at least I know their failures and their successes and I know what they can do. When you do not know who the enemy is how do you deal with it? How do you say it may be him, it may be her, it may be that, but I am not sure how to do it?
You have a number of choices. You can say that because there is no enemy that I can perceive I am not going to do anything at all. I am going to pack it up and throw it away. Or you can say that because you are not
Private Members' Business
sure who the enemy is you should do double what was done before. I am not so sure that is the right way either.
Don't do anything.

I heard a comment from my hon. colleague from Victoria who said: "Don't do anything". I would be more kind to the government. It is trying to do something. It made a policy statement on defence that would have been all right if nothing had changed since the 1987 white paper. Since the white paper all the assumptions made there were changed rapidly and dramatically. The world is not in the same place as was described in this well put together and well written document.
We have things going on in the world that we see and I am sure we recognize for what they are. Who is the enemy? We have a lot of things going on. We have a thing which the books and those who are more learned than I call cultural nationalism. We see it in our own country and it is very deep. Sometimes I believe I understand it, and when I sit down to analyse it I really do not understand it. It is not the same as putting a pilot in a MiG 34 or a MiG 26 and sending it from a to b. It is not the same as having a cruiser and putting a whole bunch of missiles on it, because the intelligence can say this is what is happening. But how does intelligence recognize cultural nationalism? It is deep. There are times when you think it is submerged that it will always return. There is cultural nationalism.
There is the instability going on in the world. I take you back, Mr. Speaker, to 1945. I say it took from 1945 until around 1950 for the people who were working on defence policies to sort them out. Our major change in defence policy came in the last couple of years when the cold war was basically over. We made a change in NATO. We arranged some of our base structures in the country. As a statement of policy this came out in the policy statement I hold in my hand. If I were defence minister, there is not a great deal different that perhaps I would have advised my Prime Minister on.
I will go back to the point of my motion. I would love to see a public debate about defence. National defence is the second largest department in the government. The industries involved in national defence involve 120,000 people and a countless number of firms. I am not going to get into the arms sales. That is a separate subject, but it certainly is related. I think my hon. friend will speak on it as a subject as well.

November 5, 1991
Private Members' Business
I suppose, Mr. Speaker, you are asking where am I going. I am surprised that nobody on the other side of the House has asked me where I am going. I am not sure where I am going. The point is there is a need for a public debate.
I come from a reasonably large riding. There are
110,000	people in my riding. It is a modest riding and one would not think it was that related to defence. I boast, and I think rightfully so, that Bonavista-Trinity-Conception is the largest fishing riding in Canada. Nobody has challenged me on that.
I have.

The hon. member for Burin-St. George's says that he has. We will sort this out later on.
I am one of 295 people in this House. I am modest enough to think that I am not much different from anyone else. In my riding there is seldom a time that I go to a reception or speak or go to a gathering where someone does not say that their son or daughter served in the Persian Gulf. They were involved. They are asking me: "Where are we going?" I say that I think we will continue to have a defence policy and I think we will continue to support defence matters. Any government, whichever side of the House, can have a defence policy. I suppose I have kind of lost track of this, but I go back to the statement of the Minister of National Defence. The day before he made his statement the Prime Minister said: "There will be a larger statement later on". I assumed that there would be some public consultation. The motion says that I would like to see some public consultation. I go back to what Sir John Hackett said. I started with Sir John Hackett. I do not mind talking about him because he was an army general and most admirals and generals usually get along. He was a veiy deep, learned man. Mr. Speaker, before you give me the option to sit down, I will once again, in closing, ask you and ask those who are going to speak on this matter to reflect on his words. Once again, John Hackett said: "What a countiy gets from its military is what they ask for. Nothing more, nothing less. When they look at their military they are looking in a mirror and, if the reflection is a true one, the face they see will be their own".
Mr. Speaker, I thank you for your indulgence.

speakeroldname: Mr. Patrick Boyer (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of National Defence):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of National Defence
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would like to congratulate the member for bringing the motion before the House today so we can again debate and consider the future directions of Canadian defence policy.
I agree with the member that it is important that these issues be raised publicly and considered from many different perspectives. Increasingly we have been having good debates here on the floor of the House of Commons about foreign and defence policy. It is a welcomed change.
I remember the week the Berlin Wall fell and Germany was reunited. There was not a single question asked in the House of Commons during Question Period relating to any aspect of Canadian foreign policy. I think we were preoccupied with a domestic tax change or some matter like that.
Therefore, it is always important as Canada is in transition from the model of a 19th century nation state into a 21st century international countiy that we the elected representatives of the people contemplate the direction that the policy should go.
The member, in the wording of his motion, wants to bring Canada's defence policy out in the open for a full public debate on the over-all logic of our defence position. "Out in the open" and "full logic" are two elements that I just want to note in passing.
The more open the better, but I think there are already a number of public meetings and discussions, not only right now on the floor of the House of Commons, but earlier today the standing committee on defence met with this whole subject as part of its current, self-assigned mandate. Elsewhere throughout the country the minister's own policy statement to which the member has referred is also part of that. Therefore I think our countiy is engaged in public discussion and the more the better. I agree with that.
As to the logic, I pause. The search for logic in government policy is perhaps a quest that would leave the hon. member mad. It is very hard sometimes to find logic. Historians tell us that Canada defies logic, that the policies of government that tried to keep this country

November 5, 1991

united east to west on an economic basis defied the logic of north-south integration.
In the member's own province of Newfoundland the constituent assembly that met to consider what questions should be put on the ballot in the referendum omitted the option of Newfoundland voting to join with Canada. There was no logic in that. In fact it was subsequently added by the British government as a choice for Newfoundlanders. As a consequence of that we have the member here today and as a consequence of that we have this debate.
The point I am making is that if our quest is for logic, I think we will be here a lot longer than the brief time allowed for this debate.
A former leader of the member's party, Mr. Trudeau, once outlined his political philosophy in an effort to have the mind rule over the heart, the head over the heart, although his political actions in many respects sometimes contradicted that. I think that we increasingly see-
You are being partisan.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of National Defence
speechtext:
The hon. member is interrupting by saying that I am being partisan. I am analysing the problem we have in public policy, that it is not always logic and the rationally designed order that prevails. People are as much if not more motivated by emotion, instinct and by primeval human drives to do things as they are by logic. I simply make the comment in passing that we should look at the broad outlines of the policy and the reasons for it. If it appears to be logical, so much the better as far as the hon. member is concerned.
He has outlined all the changes that have taken place. No one can escape them. It is in that context that the previous government's policy on defence issued in 1987 became outdated. It stood as an island trapped in time as so many other changes were swirling around. The member has referred to them.
There are not only changes in the international context, but changes domestically relating to the government's efforts to try to deal in a serious minded way with the national debt that the country has and to bring spending down. We have changed international context and budgetary restraint at home.
A third element impinging on this is the desire to have the Canadian Armed Forces indeed do more at the very
Private Members' Business
time their numbers are being reduced, to take on new roles in addition to those that are required of a professional armed force of the kind that we have in Canada.
It was on that basis that the minister made the policy statement not so long ago on September 17. He did present reasons that yes, there would be changes and yes, there would be elements remaining the same.
This should not be disparaged. This is a "logical" approach to the situation I have just described. There will be some progress. There will be some progressing and some conserving of elements that together are necessary as we go ahead in the new context.
I think that the basic tenets of Canadian defence policy are out in the open. They are very much in the open. They are part of the public record and they have been there for a long time following some three fairly well-known features. The first is defence and collective security. The second is arms control and disarmament and the third is the peaceful resolution of disputes.
Those are areas that are long-standing, publicly known and publicly supported aspects of Canadian defence policy. The call to have this out in the open is perhaps a call not so much as to reveal anew, for the first time, public policy. It is rather to invite the hon. member to remove his sun glasses and see what is there in full public display for everyone to see and recognize.
The global changes that we have seen are of historic proportion. We discussed this yesterday when the member for Victoria had a resolution before us dealing with the future role of the North American defence agreement between Canada and the United States.
The cold war is over and we are no longer viewing the role of the Canadian Armed Forces, our treaties or our arrangements in that context. Yet, to say that, we must not assume that all the sheep and all the lions are lying down in the pasture together and that there is no hostility or threat of hostility. We must not assume that there is no need for us to still maintain our vigilance, because certainly there is.
I think the ongoing conflict in Yugoslavia is ringing a very clear warning bell to the world community revealing how the many challenges that remain can lead to violence.

Private Members' Business
I had a discussion on Friday of last week with Dr. Madeleine Fullbright, Professor of International Law and a Democratic presidential adviser on foreign policy in the United States. We discussed the survey she had conducted in central and eastern Europe showing that in virtually all of the countries of central and eastern Europe a majority of the people living there feels that a part of their country is within the borders of another country.
There are a lot of possibilities over there that will give rise to peacekeeping work and a strong role for the United Nations to keep regional and border conflicts from erupting. That is one of the other areas where the policy announced by the Minister of National Defence clearly states Canada's commitment to continuing in that role. That is another part of our policy.
Indeed I would like to add personally that the work of a number of parliamentarians to see us now move to the next stage of preventive peacekeeping is something that would be a further role for Canada to provide leadership on a global basis and be consistent both with the traditions of our country and the new opportunities and challenges internationally.
There are many more elements to all of this and in a brief 10 minutes I cannot entirely reiterate the lengthy policy statement of the minister. However I would like to clarify that the government is responding in a way that is both pragmatic and creative. It is with that in mind, with more debate and discussion by Canadians on this issue, that we can have a consensus in the country on the future direction of a very constructive defence policy for our country.

Mr. Speaker, I rise to participate in this debate and join in congratulating the member for bringing forward this motion. It is clearly important that there be public debate on Canada's defence policy.
I have to say that I am very disappointed that this is as far as the motion goes, that I am very disappointed in the content of the member's speech as he brought it forward; not in his style, not in his motivation, not in his intention, but in the content and substance of it.
I think that the parliamentary secretary who just spoke is quite correct. The government's policy is quite out in the open. The government has made a policy statement. The government is conducting defence policy in this country. What this country now needs is not a quiet, wimpish motion that calls for more public debate with the Liberal Party, if I can say it, hiding again behind process. Rather, let us begin to join issue on the issues that there are in defence.
The government has put forward its position and we have put forward our position. The country is waiting perhaps with bated breath for what the Liberal Party has to say on these critical issues as the world changes.
What do you have to say?

If you will be quiet for a minute or two, you will hear exactly what we have to say. You have heard it already on two or three occasions and you will hear it again. Let me raise first of all the context in which our country now has to look at issues of defence policy. It is absolutely clear the fundamental premise that has underscored our defence policy since the late 1930s has changed, particularly the fundamental premise of our policy since the end of the Second World War and the beginning of the cold war. It is a point which I made last night in the discussion on NORAD.
The Warsaw pact has disbanded. Virtually all Warsaw pact countries regard themselves as applicants to join the west and to enter into normal peaceful relations with the NATO countries including Canada and the United States. They have laid down their arms. They present no threat. They want to be friends and allies.
The Soviet Union has been proclaimed by the former Secretary of State for External Affairs to be our friend and our ally, and we are now entering into economic, political and social relationships to make that a fact.
Both the United States and the Soviet Union are proceeding at break-neck pace to dismantle the whole nuclear apparatus that had grown up during the cold war. We are left still with the remnants of that and that needs to be dealt with, but it will not be dealt with by a build-up of arms. It will be dealt with by effective arms control and arms reduction measures.
Canada and the defence planners and public policy makers now face a complete re-vision and re-orientation of where we want to go in this country. We start with the
November 5, 1991

first question: What is the threat to Canada? What threats are there to our territory, our space and our integrity from a military point of view? The answer has to be virtually none. There is no country, other than the United States of America, that could successfully invade Canada and hold space in our country. There is the risk of occasional incursion, militarily, from some country testing and probing our area and again it is primarily the United States and the Soviet Union that have any capacity left to do that. Challenges to our sovereignty come primarily from the United States and not from anyone else. There are the remnants of Soviet power left, but that is all there is.
At the defence committee today we heard of the complete chaos in the Soviet Union which is facing transition from a state run economy to a market mixed economy, transition from a military system phasing out which employed millions of Soviets both in the defence industry and in the armed forces. That is being dismantled and it is facing the very transition of the Soviet empire into a series of republics and a very loose federation. It simply does not have the time, energy, money or drive to provide any military threat to speak of to Canada.
We happen to be in effect the Switzerland of the 20th and 21st centuries in that in the current terms no country can engage in a significant military attack against Canada. We need to patrol our coasts. We need to know what is happening in our air space. We need to have some capacity to deal with incursions and, in terms of our own territory, that is it.
The question for Canadians and the hard question for Canadians is to what extent do we contribute militarily to security in other areas of the world. The clear answer, in which all Canadians agree, is that we participate in UN peacekeeping. On that we share. I think most Canadians would agree that if the CSCE called on Canada to participate in some form of peacekeeping in Yugoslavia or in the foreseeable future in parts of the Soviet Union as it now is, where minorities may be under attack or where there are regional tensions between republics of the Soviet Union, where there are problems of that kind, Canadians would look very seriously at that.
I think we see that we have a role in a kind of peacekeeping area, but we do not come to the post cold war era as a major military power. We come as a middle power with credibility, as a negotiator with credibility, in
Private Members' Business
a role as confidence building and, most important, with credibility in terms of developmental assistance and environmental work. It seems to me that the post cold war era for Canada is going to require a very significant contribution. The role we can most effectively play is in trying to finally rid the world of poverty, to try to support the efforts of peoples of the world to build social justice, to work on the institutions of international stability, order, peace and justice such as the United Nations, the CSCE and other regional groupings.
What we need to do is take initiative. I have not heard a word from the Liberal Party on this. It is really interesting that the associate critic for the Liberal Party says he does not know where he is going in these areas. I may have taken him out of context, but we have not heard from him on issues-
I did not say that. We do not know, as a country, where we are going.

I thought I heard him say that he, too, did not know where he was going. I see the parliamentary secretary nodding vigorously. The record of Hansard will tell the tale.
The fact remains that what we should be doing is moving quickly to provide leadership on developing a polar security arrangement, on trying to de-escalate the arms build-up that there has been for the last 40 years. This is the future of debate in Canada and this is the focus of the debate. This House has to pick up the challenge and the government has to pick up the challenge of bringing Canadians into this discussion as a whole. The questions of debate now are not technical, military questions.
They are questions of public policy, of what Canada's relations should be with the United States, what our relations are with Europe, what our relations are with our neighbours. This should be the focus and these are questions of major public policy, and this has to be the focus of debate.
The citizens' inquiry on peace and security, sponsored and organized by the Canadian Peace Alliance and its constituent groups, is performing a very important service for this country and is beginning to open this up. We in this House and the government, for its part, have to build on that.

Private Members' Business
It is not sufficient for these issues to be the property of the military. The military and the Department of National Defence in this country played an enormously important role in the Second World War, in the First World War, in the Korean War, in the Persian Gulf War, and in keeping the peace over the last 40 years. But the property of this debate is not that internally of the Department of National Defence.
To this extent I entirely agree with the underlying proposition of the member who moved this motion. It is that this discussion has to be brought out of the Department of National Defence. The way in which the September paper was produced is not constructive and effective. The first questions that have to be asked are: what is the military threat to Canada? What perspectives do we have for the future? Where are we going in the future? These fundamental questions are public questions which all Canadians should be engaged in. It is our responsibility to find a forum, a process and a way for that debate to be engaged.

Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to enter into this debate knowing full well, however, that I follow people who are so well versed in the subject, the member who was a career officer from the Armed Forces from Bonavista-Trinity-Conception, the critic for defence from the NDP, and indeed the hon. parliamentary secretary to the minister of defence.
I hope during this debate to point out that perhaps we have already met the main part of this motion. There has been a great deal of room for public input. Indeed, we are probably already providing for what the member for Victoria is suggesting, that we give a place to join issue, that we let people come in and talk through the things I will mention a little further along in my speech.
Before we do that I would like to comment that the member for Bonavista-Trinity-Conception has quoted a person who said that we get from our Armed Forces only that which we ask of them, that if we look in the mirror we will see what we need from the Armed Forces. I would like to suggest that they have always delivered more than what we asked. They have always served us so well, in two world wars, in Korea and in the Middle East, more recently last year in Oka. Indeed, we are proud of everything that the Armed Forces have done for us
because they do go beyond what duty might demand of them.
Because we are coming close to November 11 and the time when we remember the sacrifices of the people who fought for Canadian values, I want to say that we will never forget what they have done in their sacrifices for Canada.
Let me move to the topic of today. I want to suggest that the recently announced defence policy was the product of in-depth research and review of opinions and views offered by numerous people and organizations since 1987. Contrary to what at least one member of the opposition party has said here today, the review was not completed in isolation. Studies and reports by various parliamentary committees on a broad range of defence subjects were taken into account. These included studies on maritime sovereignty, Canada's land forces, NORAD renewal, the gulf war and Middle East security, the arms treaty and the Oka crisis.
Many of these hearings included testimony from individual citizens as well as various organizations and interest groups. The minutes of all proceedings, as well as the final reports of these all-party committees, are public and are available to anyone interested in defence issues.
The government has also listened to the position set out by the Canadian Institute for Strategic Studies and other organizations that expressed their views. In addition, we have heard from countless other interested and concerned citizens. In fact, since the release of the white paper on defence in 1987, the public has expressed its views on defence through thousands of letters to the Minister of National Defence and the Secretary of State for External Affairs, as well as through testimony during participation in government sponsored meetings and conferences. Now that the policy has been released I may add that there continues to be ways for Canadians to influence the content and orientation of our policy.
First, an advisory group has been created to study this area of concern to many Canadians, the process for rationalization of Canadian Forces bases and installations. Members of this advisory group were selected from outside the government or any political party in order to give as much objectivity to the process as possible. Their report will be tabled publicly and will be passed to the Standing Committee on National Defence and Veterans Affairs for further review and recommendations. I might say that we in this House all know the

chairman of that particular committee, the member for Crowfoot, with his strongly independent processes, is going to make sure that everyone who wishes to give a view to that committee will be able to do so.
This process provides the public with the opportunity to scrutinize the principles, the parameters and the logic of the planned review of defence infrastructure and offer their opinions.
Second, the opportunity to discuss, review and recommend direction of our defence policies and programs is presented at least once a year when Main Estimates are referred to the Standing Committee on National Defence and Veterans Affairs, as well as at any time supplementary estimates or interim estimates for the Department of National Defence are tabled.
Upon any one of these occasions the committee may consult with concerned citizens and various interest groups, and indeed I am sure that they would like to hear from those concerned citizens and would help the committee to talk to departmental officials, and of course the Ministers of National Defence.
Reports resulting from these hearings are public and are considered by defence planners. Moreover, it is the intention to come forward with a more detailed explanation of defence policy upon the consideration of the Estimates.
Finally, as the world order is evolving so quickly, flexibility in any defence policy has become essential. Toward this end, this government is seeking more public input on future defence policy than any previous government has done.
Annual ministerial declarations will allow the government to consider public opinions, provide for greater public consultation and make appropriate policy adjustments in a timely manner. This government has in fact conducted a defence review based on the realities of the current national and world situation.
As the government continues to consider changes in defence policy, we will continue to listen to the views of Canadians. In the meantime we have produced a defence policy which meets the needs of Canada in an era of rapid change. It is a flexible policy. It is a realistic
Business of the House
policy for the people of Canada and, moreover, it is an achievable policy.

Mr. Speaker, I want to congratulate my colleague from Bonavista-Trinity-Conception in bringing forward this very timely motion this afternoon in private members' hour. I was particularly interested in hearing the defence critic for the NDP in the House get up and deliver a cheap shot at his efforts on his first go round. We in this House know that the New Democratic Party of Canada would be quite happy to have the Ottawa police force as the national army of Canada and so we write that off without worrying about it any longer.
We have to take this motion very seriously. I am glad that some of the government members are taking it very seriously because there is a great rapport on this issue in this Parliament.
While we have things moving toward peace on the international scene, and we are all very pleased with that, we have to be very concerned about the accidents of history that happen along the way. We have had those accidents of history happen in days gone by and they have caused great consternation to the human race in this world.
As we come up to Remembrance Day, I think it is even more apropos that the hon. member for Bonavista- Trinity-Conception has brought this motion forward for us to take a look at and consider what should be in a future defence policy for Canada.
We know that the white paper the government put out a few years ago is now totally out of date. It has come forward with some ad hoc suggestions which really do not serve the purpose of our times.
I totally agree with the hon. member for Bonavista- Trinity-Conception when he says that we get out of our Canadian forces what we ask of them. We have a tremendous record in the activities that we have partici-
Private Members' Business
pated in around the world. The world needs Canada. I think that is a very important thing to remember at this time when we are reviewing defence policies. The world needs Canada.
We have troops right now on the Golan Heights which have been there for some time between Syria and Israel and they have been doing an excellent job. Sometimes people forget they are even there but they are there and they are doing their job.
We have about 560 troops still in Cyprus keeping the peace in that part of the world and that has gone on for some 27 years. We do not know how much longer it is going to go on.
We had occasion to send teams of our military personnel to Vietnam at the close-out of that war where they did a super job. Korea was a UN battle to drive the communists back to the line that had been agreed upon by the United Nations. Canadians went over there and served well. We will remember those who made the supreme sacrifice in that battle when we stand around the cenotaphs at more than 1,700 Royal Canadian Legions across this country next Monday, November 11.
We have sent troops to Africa on peacekeeping missions. We have sent troops to Central America to try to manage peace or bring peace about in that area.
Our Canadian forces, as the hon. member who sponsored this motion very well knows, are not only soldiers. People look upon them as military. They are military first because they have a job to do when they are given the orders to do it. Second, they are great diplomats because they are called upon to deal with many nations of the world and other forces that they work with in peacekeeping with the United Nations.

Mr. Speaker, as I was saying before Private Members' Business started at five o'clock, the Gallup poll that was done in September 1991, as you can see, has a different slant to it than the government's piece of legislation, in particular under the area of law-abiding sportsmen, recreational shooters and collectors that should not lose their guns because of the actions of relatively few criminals. Mr. Speaker, 82 per cent of Canadians said that they agreed with that statement.
In connection with this situation we are dealing with I want to talk a little bit particularly about the motion and the area of amendment I am looking for. That is that Motion No. 4, about which we are talking particularly,
and the others that are bunched together delete all reference in clause 2 which adds the definition of a large capacity cartridge magazine.
When we dealt with C-80, and I was a member of that committee, we dealt particularly with clip size. I want to read what the committee said about that and particularly some of the individuals that came forward. One of the areas we focused on was that magazines are unmarked and thus untraceable. I cannot understand for the life of me why anybody would want to put in a piece of legislation which the experts out in the field tell us cannot be enforceable. That situation is really what we are debating here today.
What we are debating is just what it means to the law-abiding citizen, the individual who feels that this piece of legislation does absolutely nothing to the criminal element that we as members of Parliament are supposed to be dealing with.
We are not supposed to be restricting severely law-abiding citizens who are not the problem at all. I will not get much of a chance to deal with that because of the short time that I have, but I want to suggest to the members opposite that removing over two million clips and also outlawing a significant amount of firearms because of the fact that some of these clips are built in is not going to improve the situation one iota in the urban centres of this country.

Mr. Speaker, I think it is important for Canadians to look at the problems we are attempting to deal with in addressing the very important issue of arms control.
Last year there were about 1,400 deaths in Canada that were arms related. Of those, 1,100 were suicides. About 100 to 200 were from the criminal use of firearms.
This bill purports to make our society safer by dealing with the criminal use of firearms. How does it attempt to do this? First of all, it does make it more difficult for people to get an FAC, a firearms acquisition certificate. There is going to be more screening. This is good, but I am not sure that they have gone far enough in terms of these provisions.
Another area they are going to look at is restrictions on the types of arms that Canadians can have. They will do this by limiting or making restricted weapons or outlawing certain types of weapons, including guns which were automatic but which have been converted to semi-automatic. They will also limit the size of clips, the number of bullets that can be fired from certain guns. In doing so they are looking at the problem of what types of
The problem is that many gun collectors, people who belong to gun clubs and people who shoot for recreational purposes, are going to be affected because they have a number of these types of arms in their collections, legally acquired in the past. One of the problems we face is that throughout all of the hearings we have had there has been almost no suggestion and certainly no evidence that it is legitimate gun collectors and members of gun clubs who have created the problem of gun-related deaths in Canada.
As a matter of fact, these people have probably done more through training courses and rigorous screening of people who are admitted to their gun clubs to make the use of guns safe if they can ever be.
It seems to me that this bill as it now reads is dealing not with the fundamental issue of controlling the criminal use of guns. It is penalizing people who have proven in the past that they are part of the solution and not part of the problem of gun related deaths in Canada.
Does this bill deal with increased penalties for criminals who use guns in the course of a crime? For example, it was suggested by many of the lobbyists who appeared before committee that we should increase the penalties for the use of guns in crime.
We should make it mandatory that a person have at least a two year sentence for even using a gun during the course of an offence. You could say that this could create problems in terms of plea bargaining and the administration of justice. Suggestions were put forward that you could not withdraw this mandatory penalty without the consent of the provincial Attorney General. That would give a certain flexibility if you need it.
Is there anything in this bill to deal with mandatory penalties for smuggling guns into Canada? Guns smuggled into Canada are often used in crimes. Is there anything in this bill to deal with mandatory penalties for the theft of firearms? No.
If we are really attempting to deal with gun related crimes and the deaths that ensue, which none of us want to see and which we should be seeking to prevent, then I

feel that this bill is deficient in not dealing with these very important issues.
This bill is very deficient in that it is not fair. People have over the years acquired a number of guns. I do not have a gun and I do not particularly like guns but people have within the law gone out and bought collector's items and paid a lot of money for them. Many of these guns are going to be taken away from them by this bill without compensation. It is expropriation without compensation. You cannot do that in terms of peoples' homes or cars. Surely this is not fair.
Another problem I see with this bill was mentioned by the hon. member for Kenora-Rainy River who has a good knowledge of this bill and has spoken strongly on it. He will speak more. He called for mandatory training programs so that when people are going to acquire a gun, particularly for the first time, they have to learn more about safety and the safe use of these guns.
There is no provision for these mandatory training programs in this bill. How do you get at the accidental use of firearms causing serious harm to people unless you train people who are going to have guns? Even under this bill there are still going to be guns.
I know I have very little time left but I find this bill extremely deficient. It is not going after the criminal use of guns or the negligent use of guns because it is simply putting most of the burden of this bill on gun collectors and people who belong to gun clubs. Neither of those sports are ones which I feel any particular personal affinity for. But let us not pretend that we are dealing with the root causes of gun related deaths in Canada and the harm that guns can cause to Canadians when we do not deal with more training and the criminal use of guns in smuggling, theft and the commission of crimes.
Maybe there is some progress. Maybe there will be some limitation on the use of guns by making it more difficult to obtain a firearms acquisition certificate. I suspect they did not go far enough in having mandatory training programs which could have been administered by these gun clubs that are willing to do it for a very minimal fee. They already impose strict standards on their own membership.
While this bill addresses the problem of gun control, it does so in a very marginal and, in many cases, unfair way. It does not address the real problems so that we as a Parliament will have to come back to deal with those issues not too many years from now.

Mr. Speaker, I find it unbelievable that the hon. member for Kenora-Rainy River proposes such a motion, and in particular Motion No. 4 which specifically aims at authorizing again large capacity cartridge magazines in firearms.
Mr. Speaker, considering all the incidents that have occurred, this goes beyond anything you could imagine. I wonder how the hon. member was able to find someone to second such a motion. I also wonder what the hon. member for Notre-Dame-de-Grace does in the Liberal Party of Canada, considering he was the first one to go and get the petition signed by 8,000 students of La Polytechnique. He was the first one to go and get that petition, but he is nowhere to be seen here today.
I was at the Polytechnique when that tragedy occured, and I could hear Marc Lepine shoot with his semi-automatic rifle. One would have had to be an expert not to think that this was a true automatic weapon. With a 30-cartridge magazine, how can people prevent a massacre? Who needs such a weapon? Who needs a rifle with a 30-cartridge magazine? I hope no member of the House. I hope this motion was simply seconded to allow a debate and to show how far ignorance can go with proposals that are totally unacceptable.
If there is a minimum of improvement in that legislation, it is because of those weapons. Obviously, as I mentioned earlier, we will have to wait for the recommendations of an advisory committee: We will have to wait for the regulations that will be tabled by the minister and approved by the cabinet. In its present form the legislation only provides for the minister and the Cabinet to make such regulations on firearms. It is already less than minimum and it is completely unacceptable to claim that firearms with any large capacity cartridge magazine should not be prohibited or restricted.
November 5, 1991

I hope that this motion will be rejected, as well as the other ones that were grouped together following the decision of the Speaker and that were proposed by the member for Kenora-Rainy River. Several of them show a similarity; others aim at making more exceptions regarding possession of prohibited weapons. There are already thousands of prohibited weapons in Canada, and there is no real control nor safe storage, not to mention that we may not even know who their owners are.
As regards certain paramilitary and semi-automatic weapons, again those who already own such firearms will be able to keep them. That is what this legislation says. Imagine: these people will become genuine gun collectors. Would you believe that the amendments and motions made here are aimed at making it even easier for those who would be entitled to buy prohibited weapons, to use prohibited weapons and to continue to keep them?.
I call upon all the members to unanimously reject that motion.

speakeroldname: Mr. Rob Nicholson (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would not want to be sitting here while someone says to reject all of them. There are actually two government amendments here that are technical amendments.
I am sure if the member for Cape Breton-The Sydneys had a look at Motions Nos. 53 and 58 he would see that they are good technical amendments which improve this bill. I would urge hon. members to support them. With respect to the other seven, I do agree with the last speaker that the House should turn them down.
As well, I would like to clear up one misconception that may have been left with the House concerning the contents of this bill. I think the member for Willowdale said to the House that nothing is being done about smuggling in this bill. I just wanted to point out to him that there is section 95 which prohibits the importation of illegal weapons. We are increasing the penalty in that section from five years to 10 years and that deals specifically with the question of smuggling.
The member for Calgary Southwest, I might add, has been very active and interested in this subject right from
Government Orders
the start. She and I were talking about Bill C-80 and commenting on what an improved bill this is. I think all members of the House would agree that this bill is a more effective piece of legislation. I thank her and others who have made recommendations and who have been interested in this. The member pointed out to me that she thought she heard the member for Willowdale say there would be no trading within the grandfathered class. I did not hear it myself. I was checking on something else.
The hon. member is shaking his head. That is fine. I just wanted to make sure the House did know that within the grandfathered class there is trading within the members of the class under this bill.
With respect to the seven amendments by the member for Kenora-Rainy River, the gist of what he is suggesting is to strip the Minister of Justice of the ability to prohibit magazine size. While the bill does not set down any restrictions in this regard, it certainly gives the power to the minister to prohibit certain magazine clips.
The minister has announced that she would eventually formulate regulations with the following limits. For magazines for centre fire semi-automatic rifles and shotguns there would be a five-shot limit. For magazines for rim fire rifles, non-semi-automatic rifles and shotguns, there would be no limit. I have been to a number of different communities and there seems to be some confusion about that last point. The magazines for handguns would be limited to 10 shots.
I would like to point out one thing to the House. In setting those limits I have had individuals ask me how this would affect people who are involved in shooting as a sport or as a recreational activity. I want to let them know first of all that as far as our international competitiveness is concerned, no event sanctioned by the International Shooting Union will be affected by these limits. Not one event sanctioned by the International Shooting Union will be affected by these limits. As well, no competitions sanctioned by the International Olympic Committee will be affected by the proposed limits of the Minister of Justice. As I say, when hon. members are considering that I think they should keep that in mind.
I believe that most hunters use magazines with a capacity of two to four shots. That is common among hunters.

Three.

November 5, 1991
