speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
The hon. member points out to me that migratory bird hunters commonly are limited to three-shot capacities. I do not want the impression to be left with individuals who have a legitimate interest in hunting or sporting purposes that somehow the government is trying to interfere with that very legitimate pursuit.
I cannot agree with the hon. member for Kenora- Rainy River. I hope the House turns down these amendments. I can tell him that there are many Canadians who would like to see a complete prohibition of semi-automatic firearms. I can also tell him that limiting fire power is less restrictive than prohibiting semi-automatic weapons. I think hon. members should keep that in mind when considering this matter.
It is a balanced package that we have here. Except for those two technical amendments that have the support of the hon. member for Cape Breton-The Sydneys, Motions Nos. 53 and 58,1 would ask the House to reject the other seven that we are discussing in this package.

Mr. Speaker, further to the speech of hon. member for Rosemont, I would like to say a few words. If you take a look at the motions tabled by the hon. member from northern Ontario, you will notice that Motions Nos. 4, 11, 17 and 54 are designed to prevent regulating magazines when the firepower of a gun can be assessed by the capacity of the magazine it can use.
The government wants to regulate this firepower by limiting the magazines capacity to a reasonable level, depending on the needs of the users. This is an important aspect of the public protection strategy, particularly Motion No. 4 which is aimed at allowing large capacity cartridge magazines.
Members of this House just cannot vote for such motions. The firearms control coalition has done a good job with very limited means. The hon. member for Rosemont has explained them very well and they must be defeated.

Mr. Speaker, I rise to speak on this amendment of the Liberal member for Kenora-Rainy River. He would
eliminate the enabling power in this legislation for the minister to ban large capacity magazines of the type Marc Lepine used in Montreal.
The bill creates the enabling power to ban large capacity magazines through regulation. It is not done in the bill. It is going to be done by regulations. The minister, however, has indicated that she is going to propose the prohibiting of all handgun magazines that hold more than 10 centre fire cartridges and all magazines for semi-automatic long guns that hold more than five centre fire cartridges. That is what she proposes to do. The question then is: What about competition shooters? There is a legitimate objection. We have amended the bill so that there is a specific exemption for legitimate competition shooters. They need not worry.
There has been concern expressed by some firearms groups that the magazine size would apply to rifles they already have. An example would be the bolt action Lee-Enfield. An extremely rare semi-automatic rifle called the Charlton may use the Lee-Enfield magazine. The concern was that the Lee-Enfield would be caught up in the prohibition because of the possible use of the magazine in the Charlton.
I put this question specifically to the minister. The minister and the parliamentary secretary assured me directly that there was a commitment that the Lee-Enfield would not be affected. I think that disposes of two objections right there.
It seems to me that the member is wrong. It is ironic that he is opposing the proposal to ban high capacity magazines, because high capacity magazines surely are not needed for hunting. Legitimate hunters do not need high capacity magazines. They are used more in assault weapons.
It is true that some legitimate shooting competitions, particularly handguns, use large capacity magazines but that issue is addressed as I said with the exemption. As a member of the BQ said, Lepine used a 30-round magazine at the Ecole Polytechnique massacre. Three weeks ago in Texas, at that horrific massacre there, there was the use of a 17-round magazine.
Why ban large capacity magazines? Let us deal with the real issue. A ban on large capacity magazines is a
November 5, 1991

practical way of limiting fire power. "Fire power", to quote a background paper prepared for the special committee on Bill C-80, "is a combination of cartridge power, possible rate of fire and ammunition capacity". Limiting the size of a magazine is a reasonable alternative to banning semi-automatic weapons. Many semi-automatic weapons have common and legitimate uses in Canada. Rather than banning the weapon, the government has chosen to limit the fire power of semi-automatics in a way that will not interfere with hunting.
That is really the key and that is why I am opposing the Liberal motion and supporting this provision in the bill. There is a problem with an increase in firepower weapons in Canada. There must be a way of addressing such weapons that are already in the hands of Canadians.
In recent years a large number of military firearms have been in Canada from a number of eastern European and Third World countries in search of foreign currency. For example, the Norinco AK-47, a Chinese copy of the Soviet assault rifle, can be bought in Montreal for $450 according to the evidence we had in our committee.
This provision will limit the capacity of future firearms' design. Weapons are becoming more and more dangerous all the time. Even if the magazine proposal has a limited impact on existing weapons, it will have the effect of stopping future, unnecessary innovation and advanced fire power before they become a problem. It seems to me that is sufficient reason to support the proposal.
I want to close with two concerns that the member from Kenora had. It has been argued that the limit of five on semi-automatic rifles will affect built-in magazines. Images of thousands of rifles having to be destroyed have been put forward by the gun lobby. So hundreds get concerned: "My God, my gun is going to be destroyed". In fact evidence presented to our special committee suggested that in 1991 of approximately 2,600 makes and models of rifles only 28 would be affected. Some 26 of these guns are in the paramilitary class and would be prohibited or restricted in any event. Thus, of 2,600 guns only two versions of the Marlin Camp Carbine are affected. For this the Liberal member from Kenora wants to eliminate an important element of the bill. It seems to me he has not thought it through.
Government Orders
Groups have raised the issue of magazines that can be used in semi-automatic and non semi-automatic firearms. Only one firearm, the Lee-Enfield, has been identified as a problem, and I already explained how I put this question to the minister.
I listened to what the member said and I think he addressed some concerns, but I think they have been dealt with. We try to deal with them in amendments we fought for in the bill, and we got them. As I said, the alternative would be to ban semi-automatics. The government has chosen not to do that. Legitimate hunters do not need large clips. Competition shooters are exempt and so I think the amendment should fall.

speakeroldname: Mr. Dave Worthy (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Public Works):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Public Works
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I also would like to speak to this group of amendments very briefly.
I had the pleasure of working for some months on the first committee with the first speaker on this, the hon. member from Kenora-Rainy River. I can attest that he did put some very valuable time in and was a valued member of that committee.
He also represents a constituency very similar to mine which is Cariboo-Chilcotin. Many of the people in his area as well as in mine depend for their livelihood on hunting and fishing and are very definitely considered to be in those areas where there is a heavy density of gun users. In many cases they are people who depend for their livelihood and their lives on the use of weapons.
In spite of the fact that we come from similar areas, and I understand totally where his concerns are with the imposition of new rules on the law-abiding people who have up until now been very wise and very safe in the use of their weapons, they have a very real distrust and in all cases a concern for these tougher changes to regulations that will be coming out through regulations.
I think there is a distinction that the hon. member has not made. In my area, and I am sure in his, in excess of 90 per cent of legitimate hunters and sporting people would not be the least bit upset if the change in magazine size as well as many of the other changes were to occur only to new guns being purchased.
Any self-respecting hunter who suggests they need more than a five shot clip would be embarrassed about it. They totally support the idea that for hunting, high capacity clips are not required. We have already made allowances for legitimate sporting events. Even in the

November 5, 1991
Government Orders
gun community a high percentage of the people, perhaps in the high 90s, would support very tough legislation as it pertains to the magazine size in particular.
I believe the only problem comes in enforcing a change in magazine size for the existing stock that is out there. On that I share the concerns of the member for Kenora-Rainy River, but I do suggest that the changes coming down are going to be coming through regulation that we as a House and our committees will have a chance to review.
I would ask that all members of the House recognize when these changes are made that there are legitimate, law-abiding people out there who do own these weapons and that they could be made to suffer inconvenience based on what these regulations do say. Therefore, we should always keep this minority of Canadians in mind when we make those changes.

speechtext: We will now proceed to the consideration of Motions Nos. 6 and 7 which have been grouped for debate purposes.

Motion No. 6.

Motion No. 7

Mr. Speaker, so we speak on Motion No. 6 which, in relation to the new section 84(c) of the Criminal Code, will have the effect of restricting the use of modified semi-automatic arms. What we asked was that modified semi-automatic arms,
November 5, 1991

that is automatic arms that were converted to semi-automatic arms, be banned. The minister did not think it was necessary to do that. Instead, it was decided to make them restricted arms.
We might as well try to do our best with what we have in that section.
Thus, it is provided in that section that it comes into force on October 1, 1992. My motion provides that that section should come into force on May 1, 1992, that is as soon as it is reasonably possible. Naturally we will see in a moment that my colleague from the NDP asks for an even sooner date for the coming into force of this section, but that seems to me to be a little too soon for people of the government.
I thought I would be very tolerant and I agreed that May 1 would be an excellent date for that section to finally come into force. The sooner it will come into force, the sooner we will be able to control the sale of arms. That, I think, is the purpose of this section and in any case it is the purpose of my motion, that we should act as fast as possible.
Moreover, I think October 1, 1992 is a bit awkward since in Quebec-it is unfortunate that our friend from Abitibi is absent-the hunting season opens in October. I believe it would really be unwise to specify a date after the beginning of the hunting season because I understand these firearms are sometimes used for hunting. I am not too inclined to believe that is the case, but it is what I have been told. I suggest that if those weapons are really used for hunting it would not be possible to enforce such a requirement as of October 1. It would not be feasible.
Besides, those guns are assault weapons and have no legitimate use in Canada. We have been saying so for a very long time. Here is a list of groups who have also claimed the same thing for a long time.
The petition circulated by the students of the Polytechnique asked for the banning of such guns. Furthermore, the Canadian Association of Chiefs of Police, the Canadian Police Association, the Canadian Bar Association, the Canadian Criminal Justice Association, the Caucus of Mayors of Major Cities, the Solicitor General of Alberta, the Chief Firearms Officers for British Columbia and Alberta, the National Association of Women and the Law, the Coalition for Gun Control and the Comite
Government Orders
pour le controle des armes de Polytechnique have all asked for the banning of those firearms.
Of course, it is obvious that unfortunately their calls were not heeded. Since we are stuck with that section because the Conservative government did not want to listen to people, we ask that at least it proceed as fast as it can.
I also wanted to say that converted automatic weapons, or modified semi-automatic weapons as they are called, were declared illegal by a Court of Appeal in at least one province. We could say that in that case there is an unfortunate regression. While the rest of the bill represents a big step forward, in the case of converted automatic weapons it goes against the decision of the Court of Appeal of one province.
I would also like to say a few words about those who object to a stricter control on firearms. Here is a really remarkable piece of literature. It is a letter that I received from the National Arms Collectors' Association. In that letter, the Association mentions that it also represents the National Firearms Association, the Ontario Federation of Anglers and Hunters, the Ontario Arms Collectors Association, the International Practical Shooting Association and the Shooting Federation of Canada.
The association writes that it represents all those people. The letter is addressed to all the members of the legislative committee which studied Bill C-17. In that letter the association tells those members that, if they vote in favour of the bill, in the next election it will do everything it can to remind Canadians of the terrible and ungrateful thing they did to the people who had elected them so generously.
It is a form of threat that I find unacceptable in 1991. It is unfortunate that such a letter was sent to the committee members. I do not think those people had the nerve to send it to all members of this House.
Of course the letter was in English. They are unilingual, that is for sure, but I could just read it to you. The sentences are a bit long. I would say it is not well written.
I will not quote the text literally but I think that I explained its content, namely the threats made to members of Parliament who would decide to vote against Bill C-17.
I do not think that the Conservative members will be intimidated. I believe that they are strong enough to vote

Government Orders
according to their conscience and I am convinced that they will not let themselves be influenced like that.
Those of us who are concerned, I mean the people who are not afraid of the National Arms Collectors' Association, asked that the legislation provide storage standards. Unfortunately, again, we will not have those standards in the act; they will be included in the regulations. We made all kinds of compromises and we tell ourselves that we will make another one.
We know it is important that it should be done through regulations, since it cannot be done directly through the act. I talked to people I know and they told me that, unfortunately, they store their firearms without unloading them. It is inconceivable, but these things happen. We must have regulations. Obviously we will not be able to check every house, but that is not the objective. The objective is to make people aware. That is what is important.
In conclusion I want to say that it was also necessary to make the population understand that having a firearm is not a right but a privilege. This is not the United States where the right to own a firearm is enshrined in the Constitution. Indeed, the second amendment gives the right to Americans. We are not in the United States. This is Canada and the bill shows that, without saying it explicitly as we would have liked. In any case we will again make a compromise and accept that legislation.
Those are the comments I wanted to make on these motions.

Mr. Speaker, I would like to speak to my motion on this matter. The motion standing in the name of my hon. friend from Saint-Hubert, who just spoke, and my motion are grouped together for debate.
What happened was that this bill was supposed to come into effect. It deals with converted automatics. The whole point of this bill is that these military assault weapons are flowing across the border. They normally would have been prohibited because they were automatic weapons but people converted them to semi-automatics to get around the law and they flooded into Canada. The government does not want these guns in Canada. That was one of the biggest parts of this bill.
In committee the government moved to extend the deadline for registering existing converted automatics. You can keep these guns now if you register them. The deadline was moved from December 31,1991 to October 1, 1992, a full eight months.
My friend proposes amendments that would bring that deadline back to May 1. My amendment would bring it back to March 1, 1992.
Just before I get into that part of it, I would like to say that I had a motion that would have eliminated entirely the grandfathered clause for converted automatics. Converted automatic weapons are remodelled to get around our present law prohibiting automatic weapons. There is no place for these weapons in Canada. They should be prohibited and an amnesty should be offered for a limited time period so that they get right out of Canada.
Mr. Lome Newson, chief firearms officer for British Columbia, said in a brief to our special committee: "In the first place these people were very much aware", that is people who were bringing these guns in, "that they were skirting the law by buying superficially modelled machine guns. They are deserving of no sympathy".
Converted automatics are treated as illegal weapons today, for the most part. There is real concern, as a matter of fact, that this provision in this bill will weaken and overturn our case law. I point to the case of The Queen v. Global Arms.
My amendment to cut this grandfathering was supported in the committee by the Polytechnique students, the Canadian Association of Chiefs of Police, the Canadian Police Association, the Canadian Bar Association, the Canadian Criminal Justice Association, the Big City Mayors Caucus, the Solicitor General of Alberta, the National Association of Women in Law, the Coalition for Gun Control and many others. I am sorry the government did not listen to them.
Let me turn to the particular amendment that I have proposed to reduce the deadline to March 1, 1992. The government extended the deadline for registered

converted automatics, that is the grandfather clause, from December, 31 to October 1, 1992. My amendment would limit this extension to March 1, 1992. The government argued that it would give people more time to learn about the proposal and to register their weapons. It also gives them more time to obtain the weapons. The history of this proposal seems to contradict it by saying no more can come in. Why? Because the government said no more can come in. You have to have a law, my friend, to say that. You cannot just say no more can come in. You could bring them in and say "you can't seize these, Mr. Customs Officer, give me the law. There is no law." The law here will be in this bill. That is a nice pious wish but that is not the law.
The history of this proposal seems to contradict what the government is doing. In May 1989 then justice minister Doug Lewis announced the government would ban converted automatic weapons. In June 1990, another year later, this Minister of Justice, the present minister, tabled Bill C-80 which prohibited converted automatics and the minister said they would have to be registered by June 1991. That was four months ago.
Bill C-80 died. The minister then tabled this bill, Bill C-17, in June. She said the deadline for registering existing weapons would be December 31, 1991. Then in committee she extended the deadline to October 1992.
Surely enough is enough. Owners of converted automatics have known about this proposal for two and a half years. It will be three and a half years by the time October 1992 rolls around. There is no need for more delay. My motion would give people enough time to register their weapons without any more needless delay. It is outrageous that the government has extended the deadline. If we are going to get serious about gun control and these guns flowing across the border into some of our large cities and causing crime in some of these cities, we have to act now.

speakeroldname: Mr. Rob Nicholson (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, first of all I am very pleased that both hon. members want to see the government's legislation enacted as soon as possible. With that sentiment I am in agreement. The question is just when is it a reasonable time for us to have this new regime up and running. It is not just for the gun owners that we are proposing the date that we are, it is for the police and the people who must administer this.
Government Orders
I have been involved with this area for the last couple of years, and neither I nor any member of the government has any interest in delaying it. We want to pick a time that is realistic. We have guns here now that will have to be registered, guns that will have to be inspected and people who will want to be a part of the grandfathering clause may have to set themselves up as genuine gun collectors. We have already agreed, the committee agreed, that there would be genuine gun collectors. People who are converting their guns will have to make sure that it is properly converted because they do not want the thing seized later. That is why we are suggesting this. We expect this bill to be passed by Christmas and we want to give ourselves, the public, the police and everyone else about nine months.
Nobody benefits from having the police swamped in the first two months, as they would be under this bill by people trying to register their firearms, people trying to get them inspected, making sure that they have been properly converted and getting themselves registered as genuine gun collectors. This system could not possibly operate in its first few months.
We do pick a realistic day. We have suggested October 1992 which will put everyone on notice. I want to assure the hon. member for Port Moody-Coquitlam because he made reference to the fact that converted automatic weapons have been coming into Canada from the United States.
I can tell him that customs officials are stopping the importation of additional firearms.
Which law is it?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
They are basing it on the court decision in Alberta, the Global Armaments case. As the hon. member knows, there is another decision in the province of Ontario that perhaps was not entirely favoured. In any case, Canada Customs has stopped the flow of these types of firearms into Canada.
It seems to me that before the court process goes any farther we should get this bill passed because I think it clarifies what it is we are prohibiting in Canada. I think it complements the existing judicial interpretation up to this point.
I do not want people to be left with the impression that somehow these things are pouring across the border. They are not. On the other hand, we have to pick a date

Government Orders
that is reasonable to have this whole regime up and running.
If some members say they do not want the grandfathering clause, I can see how we might have a system in three months in which everything is just being seized and destroyed presumably without compensation. Perhaps that might be another amendment.
We have agreed that there will be a grandfathering provision. We are setting up a regime. We are notifying people what it is we want, and there is no point to having the police and everyone else involved with this swamped with a hopeless situation in two or three months that they cannot possibly administratively handle.
I think it is better to pick a realistic date which October 1, 1992 is. I hope the House will reject both these amendments.

Madam Speaker, I am sorry to hear what the hon. parliamentary secretary to the Minister of Justice has to say. If the problem is the transition period, because of the grandfather clause that lets owners keep altered firearms, this bill could be brought into force sooner to prohibit acquisition of more firearms. After that date, offenders could have a transition period, a kind of 48-hour notice like the one for a defective light on a car. But it would be more reasonable to have a two-to three-month notice.
This bill allows people to continue to buy firearms and maybe buy more, especially for the new hunting season next fall. If the acquisition of new firearms were prohibited this coming spring, there would be no problem.
Unfortunately, the hon. parliamentary secretary has already made up his mind. He is not listening. Maybe I should switch to English. His argument is obviously faulty. What we want to do is to prohibit the acquisition of new firearms of this type as soon as possible, because we were unable to ban them altogether.

Madam Speaker, these motions aim essentially at changing the deadline for registration of converted semi-automatic weapons. The
deadline would be October 1, 1992, according to the bill, and Motions Nos. 6 and 7 suggest advanced dates.
Is it reasonable to give eight to nine months to those who until the law is passed are perfectly legitimate owners of these weapons, to register them in order to be allowed to continue their peaceful possession?
These weapons cannot be registered before the law is passed and they must be inspected before registration.
For me, October 1 is a difficult date. In the north of each province, in Quebec, for example, and in some parts of the south, October 1 is hunting time. In Quebec the hunting season begins often around October 15 for bow hunting and around October 25 or 26 for rifle hunting. For me, this date is a problem. It must advanced.

speakeroldname: Mrs. Barbara Sparrow (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of National Health and Welfare):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I just wanted to take a few minutes to say a few words with regard to Bill C-17 and the couple of amendments on the floor right now.
My involvement with firearms legislation has gone on for a number of years and indeed before Bill C-80 was tabled a year or two years ago. I have spent quite a bit of time meeting with the Calgary Police Force, the gun club personnel of southern Alberta, competitive shooters, gun associations, and firearms dealers throughout the province of Alberta. These people have been very concerned with regard to any changes in the old firearms legislation, but of course public safety is first and foremost in everybody's mind.
One thing that crops up in Alberta has to do with citizens' rights and a law that will have an effect upon sincere, law-abiding citizens and no affect upon the criminals. Madam Speaker, as you well know, within the legislation there are three or four clauses that discuss the careless handling of firearms, the storage of firearms, importing or delivering prohibited weapons and making automatic firearms. The penalties have been strengthened and we are coming down harder on the criminals, but as the parliamentary secretary has said the administration of justice is under provincial jurisdiction.
November 5, 1991

I know that the Minister of Justice has been working with the attorneys general and I would hope that these more severe penalties would come into force appropriately.
I also have to make a comment with regard to people saying that we are banning, eliminating or removing certain types of target ammunition. The bill does allow Orders in Council or the Minister of Justice to prohibit certain types of ammunition, but the only one that I am aware of is the cop killer bullets, the one that pierces the armour of our police officers. Any further prohibition would have to be put forth in the regulations and would come before this House for debate.
The time that the hon. member for Saint-Hubert asked for it to come into force was May 1, 1992 and the bill stipulates October 1, 1992. There are many Canadians who own firearms, store them extremely safely and are law-abiding citizens. We have to come forth with the regulations that will define a legitimate collector and bring forth the safety regulations with the FAC. This is another area, the firearms acquisition certificate. Anybody, after this law comes into force, who is purchasing a new weapon will have to have an FAC. We will have safety regulations. We are presently working with the various provinces, the gun clubs and the professional people to set up a type of schooling so people, prior to purchasing new weapons, will have to prove their knowledge of firearms and their ability not only to store it safely, carry it safely, shoot it safely, but know all the working parts of it. I must say that I have worked a year and a half or two years with regard to this. I know there are a lot of concerned citizens in my riding and right across Canada. The charter of rights certainly protects all citizens. There will be no search and seizure or people knocking at your door demanding to see the firearms. That is not what the bill says at all. It says that they would want to have the ability to review the collectors, the types of firearms the collectors had and whether they meet the criteria. This can be arranged on a very friendly basis. There is no such thing as search and seizure as some people are saying.
I would like to say that I am a hunter. I have been for years and years and I do own shotguns. I have four youngsters. Mind you, they are all grown up but they have grown up in a house where there were shotguns. They were all taken to gun clubs. They were taught the safety of these shotguns. They were taught how to store
Government Orders
them, how to take them apart and how to clean them, because they have to clean my shotgun. That is part of the deal. We do have safe storage in our house. The shotguns are stored in a gun case with a lock and key. Our guns are always clean. The chambers are empty and indeed are left open at all times. I cannot say that I have done everything perfectly, but there is one thing that my youngsters have learned, that they treat a gun as if it is always loaded. You never ever point a gun at anyone; the gun is always loaded. Indeed, touch wood, we have been very successful so far.
I must say that I am very proud of them. I do believe that a lot of my fellow constituents are safety conscious, understand and know the operation of shotguns. In no way is this bill going to prohibit or limit their ability to enjoy migratory shooting.
What we have moved in is the safety of Canadians all along since the last firearms legislation. I just learned today that since 1896 we have had firearms legislation in Canada. Owning a firearm is a privilege. It is not a right, as the hon. member mentioned earlier. We have had firearms in this country for about 94 or 95 years. It is a privilege, not a right.
I support the bill. A year and a half ago I had a lot of qualms, difficulties and concerns. Bill C-17 is far improved over Bill C-80.
The minister listened.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext: The minister did listen to us. In no way are we coming down against the honest, law-abiding citizens. Criminals have been targeted. We will work with the attorneys general. The penalties are stiffen It is up to the provinces to implement those penalties. I think we can see a much safer society where we all respect one another.

Mr. Francis G. LeBlanc (Cape Breton Highlands- Canso) proposes that:
Motion No. 12.
That Bill C-17 be amended in Clause 4 by adding immediately
after line 16 at page 6 the following:
"(3.3) Subsection (1) does not apply to a person who is in possession of a firearm that is a prohibited weapon by virtue of paragraph 84(l)(c) or an order made under paragraph 84(l)(e) and who lawfully disposes of the firearm thirty days after paragraph 84(l)(c) comes into force or the order is made, as the case may be, provided the firearm was lawfully possessed by that person before that time.
(3.4) Subsection (2) does not apply to motor vehicule in which there is a firearm that is a prohibited weapon where by virtue of subsection (3.3), subsection (1) does not apply to the person who is in possession of that weapon."-
He said: Madam Speaker, I appreciate the opportunity to speak for my amendment, Motion No. 12. This amendment, like the others that I proposed, aims at reinforcing the legislation and has been motivated by representations that I received during the development of this bill from citizens of my constituency.

My constituents in Cape Breton Highlands-Canso, like all Canadians, support strong effective gun control legislation. This includes experienced hunters, competition shooters and weapons collectors who responsibly purchase and use weapons for sport or for pest control.
They abhor the kind of tragedies that occurred at the Ecole Polytechnique. They want to end the criminal use of firearms to kill innocent Canadians, but they do not believe that restricting the use of certain firearms by itself will achieve this objective.
Our law enforcement, our criminal justice and our parole systems have to act to protect the victims of crime and to deter criminal activity. Training should accompany the use of firearms. Regrettably training has been insufficiently addressed in this legislation.
As well hunters and sportsmen, particularly those living in rural areas, want to feel that every effort is being made by the government to recognize and understand their particular situation. Many of the new elements in Bill C-17 are seen by the hunting and sporting community in my riding as creating an inconvenience or intrusion on their activities. I think we all acknowledge that gun owners will be inconvenienced. We all acknowledge as well that this is a price worth paying for making firearms in Canada much safer.
There are limits to what legal gun owners can and should be asked to do. We are asking that they meet a host of new FAC requirements and that they meet conversion and safe storage standards, which have not even been determined yet let alone made known to the general population. We are asking that they comply with regulations that will prohibit some of the guns which they purchased legally in good faith and often at great expense.
As drafted Bill C-17 requires those in possession of weapons prohibited by this legislation to turn in those weapons as soon as the bill is proclaimed as law or be liable to imprisonment for up to 10 years.
I believe this is unnecessarily rigid. I believe that granting at least a 30-day grace period following the proclaiming of the legislation to enable owners to dispose of their weapons properly would be appropriate and would help alleviate the perceived unfairness by some gun owners of certain elements of this law.
Many constituents have written to raise concerns about becoming criminals overnight as a result of this legislation. For example, C. S. Halet of Country Harbour has written to say: "Many hunters and gun owners are not criminals and do not want to be made ones by new firearm restrictions".
November 5, 1991

Gun owners whose weapons have been declared prohibited will need some time to make the necessary decisions. They will have to ask themselves several questions: "Can I convert my weapon?" Perhaps, but conversion standards have not been determined yet. "Should I sell my gun to a genuine gun collector?" Maybe, but this is a new element to firearms control and it will take a little time to organize a structure and a system through which these guns may pass.
"Should I turn my weapons in to the authorities?" Perhaps a great deal of money was spent on these weapons. "I live many miles from the nearest firearms officer. Should I take the chance of being caught with a prohibited weapon in the trunk of my car while taking it to hand it in?" Technically you are a criminal or you are committing a crime. But if a 30-day grace period existed, you would be free to travel to local authorities when you can to remit your gun.
Gun owners will need time to think, decide and act. Once a new regulation comes into force prohibiting guns, the present owners of these guns who bought them legally and in good faith are now violating the law. With a 30-day grace period they would have time to dispose properly of the guns and avoid becoming criminals. Even if they are not apprehended by police, they feel in their hearts that they are criminals and that is offensive to them.
If they are stopped by authorities they face up to 10 years in prison. Is this fair? Police usually unofficially allow this kind of grace period but they have the authority to enforce the letter of the law if they so wish.
I want to change the letter of the law to protect honest Canadians. Most gun owners are not criminals and we must give them every opportunity to avoid becoming criminals.
There is one final but important point I would like to make. I originally submitted this amendment as a point of reference in the legislation to accommodate my proposed motion dealing with financial compensation. That motion would oblige the government to provide fair compensation, determined by regulation, to gun owners who have to turn in weapons because they have been declared prohibited. The amount of compensation would
Government Orders
be determined by regulation in accordance with fair market values for these weapons.
Financial compensation was called for by virtually all letters I received on this bill. It was recommended by the special committee studying Bill C-80, the predecessor legislation. It would encourage compliance with the law. It would act to prevent a black market in these weapons and it would be fair to gun owners who purchased these weapons in good faith.
Unfortunately financial compensation is not provided for in Bill C-17 so my motion has been declared outside of the scope of the bill by Mr. Speaker's ruling. I have no quarrel with that ruling but I do believe the absence of a provision for financial compensation is a substantial weakness in this legislation and I would urge the government to correct this weakness in subsequent legislation.
In any case, the 30-day grace period provided for by my proposed motion would by itself be an act of good will toward legitimate owners of now prohibited weapons. I believe it would facilitate and encourage the safe withdrawal of these weapons from circulation, which is the purpose of the legislation. I hope all members will support my motion.

speakeroldname: Mr. Rob Nicholson (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I am not in support of the hon. member's motion because I think it is unnecessary. There is a provision in the current bill for an amnesty power that I think provides more flexibility to the Minister of Justice. She has indicated her willingness to use it. She can declare an amnesty for periods longer than 30 days. So on that count alone, I do not think it is necessary.
To be more specific and use an example, in the case of a firearm that was prohibited by an Order in Council, the procedure we have set out in this bill will take care of that. Hon. members will remember that at the committee stage we agreed to an amendment that would allow for the pre-publication of regulations. Now if we were prohibiting a certain type of firearm the pre-publication itself puts people on notice of the government's intention. The hon. member would know that when we set a date for proclamation there is a bit of a delay between the time we pass it and the time it is proclaimed. We are giving notice again on a second count to anyone who might be affected.

November 5, 1991
Government Orders
The hon. member knows of the discussion that we just had on the last two amendments about the closing date for the case of converted automatic weapons. We have set that at October 31, 1992. It seems to me that whether it is the amnesty or the pre-publication of the regulations that might prohibit a weapon, as well as the postponing of the closing of a class for converted automatic weapons, that the bill itself now has more provisions, and I think provides greater flexibility.
I say with respect to the hon. member that I do not think his amendment is necessary.

Madam Speaker, I listened to my colleague, the member for Cape Breton-Highlands-Canso present his amendment which I think is very important, quite in order and necessary. It is a concern among the population of Canada that when this bill comes into effect they will be considered to be breaking the law.
It is of considerable concern to a great many people. He mentioned the people in his riding. I can assure you there are law-abiding citizens in my riding and in other ridings right across this country who want to feel and know that they are doing the right thing.
The hon. parliamentary secretary has stated that there is provision for an amnesty in Bill C-17. But there is no assurance that an amnesty is going to be called right away, so the minister has that discretion.
The discretion is that she can call an amnesty whenever she thinks the amnesty is in the best interests of the country. That is a subjective decision of hers and more broadly probably the government's.
The parliamentary secretary has also stated that when the bill is proclaimed there is a period of time before the proclamation when the regulations are brought forward after they are recommended by the department. If I am not mistaken it is before they go to cabinet, which is important.
These points are true. While they are important, there is still this period of time when the bill comes into effect, when people of this country want to be assured that they have time to turn in these firearms and not be considered to be breaking the law.
I think a period of time is important. The hon. member for Cape Breton-Highlands-Canso has been very reasonable in asking for only one month. I think one month would certainly be suitable. I do not think he is
asking too much of this House and of the government to have this one month period.
He also mentioned an amendment which he brought forward which was ruled out of order regarding compensation for the firearms that are being prohibited. We may find these firearms offensive. We may find the semi-automatics that can be converted to fully automatics offensive and we may say that people should not have purchased them.
Perhaps they should have even known that sooner or later they would become unlawful. That is not the point. The point is that these people purchased these firearms when these guns were within the law. They had every right to purchase these guns. They were doing so because these were advertised in this country for sale. They purchased them and were quite within their rights and within the law to do so.
Now we are saying that they have to turn in these firearms which they purchased lawfully. Some of them are worth $700 and $800. If we want this bill to work the way we feel it should, we are asking these people to turn in a piece of their personal property. Perhaps it has sentimental value but it is valuable to them certainly through the sheer weight of the money they spent to purchase this item. We are asking them to turn it in for nothing.
That is asking a lot. I do not know of a precedent for this, unless we look at the last time that an amnesty for firearms was brought forward. We know what happened then. A lot of the firearms and automatics at that time were not turned in. In fact they are still wrapped in burlap on top of a shed or a barn or under a floor board somewhere.
They were not turned in because no one was going to turn them in. A lot of people were not going to turn them in without adequate compensation or at least even partial compensation.
There are people who say: "If we pay for these firearms, then we are inviting illegal firearms to come in from the United States into Canada and then be sold in the amnesty. We are paying the cost for illegal firearms that entered the country through the back door".
I do not think that this is reasonable if we have an amnesty of an exact period of time. I think we have to give these people the right to some compensation for their firearms. I just want to say that I think this is a good amendment. I would have hoped that the government
November 5, 1991

would have supported it, and I still hope the government will.

Madam Speaker, I would just like to make a few comments as well about this amendment that has been brought forward regarding in effect property rights, that is when somebody owns a gun that the government decides should be turned back to them.
When I think about the recent constitutional proposals that were brought forward in terms of property rights, where the government in fact is looking at fair and just compensation for any takeover of property, we could look very, very soundly and strongly at a real correlation here in terms of taking back weapons that people have paid their own money for and which is their own personal property and has been acceptable up until this point.
When we think about the Minister of Justice, which the parliamentary secretary referred to, in terms of granting amnesty for 30 days or whatever, I would think that we are probably being witnessed tonight by people watching this on television who own some of these guns and who are asking: "Why is it I should turn this back in?" How is it that the Minister of Justice would be able to grant amnesty purely on a subjective basis, if she decided to do this or not. What are there in terms of rules and regulations? What further then do we see for Order in Council regulations being put?
People from my riding are expressing concern about this very issue, as well as the whole broader scope. When this legislation is put in place, what will become of all the regulations that will be put in place simply by Order in Council? People are feeling frustrated about that. I know that I have been swamped by correspondence from people who are concerned about what is going to happen in terms of actual regulations, because they are not dealt with in the legislation, There is a certain frustration about that. As well as this idea, when people are collectors it is very near and dear to their hearts what will happen to this personal property of theirs. I think somehow the government should be thinking about intertwining the two; constitutional proposals about property rights as well as what will happen when these people have to give over weapons that they have had
Government Orders
which are worth a great deal of money and sentimental value to them as well.
I would suggest that the government think seriously about accepting this motion.

speakeroldname: Hon. Alan Redway (Don Valley East) moved:
speechtext:
Motion No. 13A
That Bill C-17 be amended in Clause 4 by adding immediately after line 16 at page 6 the following:
"(3) The said Act is further amended by adding immediately after section 90 thereof, the following section:
"90.1 (1) Where, pursuant to paragraph 90(3.2)(a), a local registrar of firearms refuses to authorize in writing that a person is a person who may possess a prohibited weapon referred to in that paragraph for use in conjunction with a firearm that is suitable for use in shooting competitions designated by the Attorney General, the local registrar of firearms shall notify the person in writing of the refusal and the reasons for it and include in the notification a copy of this section.
(2)	A person who has received a notification referred to in subsection (1) may, within 30 days after receiving the notification or within such time as is, before or after the expiration of that period, allowed by a provincial court judge, request in writing the local registrar of firearms to refer the matter to a provincial court judge having jurisdiction in the territorial division in which the person resides.

Government Orders
(3)	On a reference by the local registrar of firearms pursuant to subsection (2), the provincial court judge shall fixa date for the hearing of the reference and direct that notice of the hearing be given to the person and to the local registrar of firearms, in such manner as the provincial court judge may specify.
(4)	In a hearing under subsection (3) the burden of proof is on the person to satisfy the provincial court judge that the refusal was not justified.
(5)	Where at the conclusion of the hearing under subsection (3), the person has satisfied the provincial court judge that the refusal was not justified, the provincial court judge shall, by order, direct the local registrar of firearms to authorize in writing that the person may possess a prohibited weapon referred to in paragraph 90(3.2) for use in conjunction with a firearm that is suitable for use in shooting competitions designed by the Attorney General and the local registrar of firearm shall immediately comply with the order.
(6)	Where a provincial court judge makes an order pursuant to subsection (5), the local registrar of firearms may appeal to the appeal court against the order and the provisions of Part XXVII except sections 816 to 819 and 829 to 836 apply, with such modifications as the circumstances require, in respect of the appeal.
(7)	In this section "appeal court" has the meaning given that expression in subsection 100(11)."
He said: Madam Speaker, like all members of the House, I have been the recipient of a great many representations from people on both sides of this bill. Many people for and many people against this bill have put forward to me their concerns and their thoughts, and in each and every case I have made those known to the minister and as many as I could to the committee when it was sitting considering the bill itself. There were a number of suggestions made to me that I thought certainly should be incorporated in the bill and I had put forward a number of amendments to the bill. Unfortunately all but one of those has been ruled out of order by The Speaker, and so I have been left with this one amendment before the House this evening.
I might just say however that one of the other amendments in particular it seemed to me made imminent sense in light of the fact that Canadians are concerned about fighting criminals with guns and concerned about public safety. Surely the kind of legislation that we should be bringing forth here is legislation aimed at that sort of thing.
With that in mind, I did put forward an amendment which would have required where evidence became known to law enforcement officers that a firearm had been used in the commission of an alleged criminal offence, that a firearms charge would have to be laid in addition to all other charges and that where such a
charge was laid the charge could not be withdrawn at a subsequent time once it had been laid. Unfortunately, that has been ruled out of order and is not before the House tonight.
I would hope that the government in its wisdom would introduce legislation of that sort veiy shortly after dealing with this bill.
The motion that is before the House tonight, however, in my name-and I thank the hon. member for Lethbridge for his second and his work in relation to this motion and amendment-creates an appeal process where, from a decision of the local Registrar of Firearms, where under the provisions of the bill as it now stands, the local registrar may allow a person, who is competing in a shooting competition, someone who has already received a firearms acquisition certificate, probably a member of a gun club, someone who has received all sorts of training on the weapon and is good enough to be competing in a shooting competition that has been authorized by the Attorney General of the province, to use a large capacity cartridge magazine. The local registrar can agree to that or he can reject it. If he agrees, he has to issue an authorization in writing and, if he does not issue that authorization in writing, then the person who wishes to compete using a large capacity cartridge magazine does not have the right to do so.
The decision then in the bill is an arbitrary one and at present there is no right to appeal that decision. My amendment would provide a right to appeal that provision to a provincial court judge and so forth in the same fashion with the same kind of an appeal process as is included in the bill already with respect to appealing decisions concerning firearms acquisition certificates. There is, as I have indicated in the bill, an appeal process where a firearms acquisition certificate has been refused for the person who has been refused to appeal that decision. This amendment would provide exactly the same appeal provisions with respect to someone who was turned down from receiving written authorization to use the large capacity cartridge magazine in a shooting competition that was authorized by the Attorney General.
It seems to me only reasonable that if we are going to allow this appeal procedure in relation to an FAC we should also be allowing it in this case as well. I understand that the government is prepared to consider this in
November 5, 1991

a positive vein and I would urge all members of the House to adopt this amendment.
Madam Speaker, that sounds like a reasonable amendment and I would support it.

Madam Speaker, I must say I was speaking to the hon. parliamentary secretary about this motion and I was kidding him about it. Quite seriously, this motion is reasonable and we certainly would be prepared to support it.

Madam Speaker, I would like to thank the hon. member as well for a very reasonable and thought out motion. I would like to again encourage other government members to support that as well. I think it is excellent.

Motion No. 19
That Bill C-17 be amended in Clause 9 by striking out line 28 at
page 10 and substituting the following therefor:
"(3) Paragraph 97(4)(d) of the said Act is repealed and the following substituted therefor:
"(d) comes into possession of a firearm by operation of law and within a year thereafter, lawfully disposes of it or obtains a firearms acquisition certificate under which he could have lawfully acquired the firearm; or."
"(4) Subsection 97(4) of the said Act is".
He said: Madam Speaker, my motion is No. 19 and I will be speaking at great length later on in this debate, I guess it will be tomorrow, about my feelings on the bill.
I know full well that tomorrow night or Thursday morning this bill will pass.
I must say at the outset, however, that during my short term as a member of Parliament, just coming up to three years now, I do not think I have ever seen a piece of legislation like this that is so flawed and a piece of
Government Orders
legislation that tries to do something that I do not think it is successful in doing.
I believe this is nothing but a bill to hoodwink the Canadian people into believing that the government is concerned about or trying to do something about gun control when it clearly is not.
If this bill is real gun control, then it must address gun control in four different areas. It must address the accidental use of firearms in domestic violence and suicide, and most important, in crime. This bill addresses none of these uses of a firearm, except by placing more stringent conditions on the acquisition of an FAC.
I believe people all across Canada are cynical and sceptical of their political leaders, not only because of the stands they take on one side of an issue or another, or on their political philosophy, whether it is from the left or the right.
They are upset with politicians because they feel they are not willing to take the tough decisions. They are not willing to come to grips with the real problems.
A real problem is the misuse of firearms in our communities, especially in urban centres.
We were talking earlier today about the GST. This is a prime example of where the government saw a need for money. People were crying for real tax reform and the government, instead of bringing in real reform, went to a tax gab instead.
I see this as a similar bill. It fails to address the real problems in our society. It gives Canadians a false sense of security that the government is actually doing something to stop violent crimes when in fact it is not.
I would suggest that in this bill the government is encouraging an underground network of illegal guns. If we as a society deem that we do not want certain guns, there are a couple of ways of getting rid of them. The government can use its heavy hand and come in and grab them and say: "We deem these to be not in the public's interest and we will take them". On the other hand it can invest in a system whereby it makes sure it gets those guns back.
A lot of these guns are very expensive. I do not believe that Canadians will be so willing to give these guns back. That is why I have put forward amendments to this bill similar to those put forward by my friend from Cape

November 5, 1991
Government Orders
Breton Highlands-Canso which would mandate the government to compensate these individuals.
The question I am talking about in this amendment deals with the situation of an elderly person who is a collector of guns and who becomes deceased. The guns then are left to his family. As the bill reads, and as the act is now, we are in a quandary. If the spouse does not have an FAC then legitimately the government can come in and take all that property. We could be talking about thousands and thousands of dollars.
What I want to do in this amendment-I say one year thereafter but I am willing to accept any amendments to that, whether it be three months or more-is give individuals some time whereby they could dispose of these assets or get an FAC. Right now persons would have to wait 28 days to get an FAC if they did not own one.
Legitimately this person will be holding illegal guns. I think this aspect was debated in committee but unfortunately it was never dealt with and the committee never really came up with any solution to a situation like this. I have talked to the parliamentary secretary about it and hopefully he will be able to talk to the minister about it and tiy to make some changes in the bill, whether it is through another act or through regulation.
In my last few minutes I want to take the opportunity to talk a bit about what some of my constituents have been saying because I, like other members of Parliament, have been inundated with letters from constituents about this. Remember that I am in a rural area. I think there are a lot of rural people who have legitimate concerns about this bill and how it will affect their lifestyles.
There is one gentleman who happens to be a gun collector. He says: "I would require genuine gun collector status which would be refused unless I consented to periodic inspections. It is curious that an honest citizen must open their door and have their privacy invaded. Yet a criminal's privacy is protected by the use of a search warrant or some other such device. There are too many non-defined areas that will be filled in after the bill's passing. For example, what will be prohibited? What is safe storage? This demonstrates no regard for the financial loss or limitation of real personal property to an honest citizen". That is one of the areas in which I tried
to deal with an amendment. However, it was ruled out of order by the Speaker.
He states further: "C-17 creates a permanent jungle for the use of a firearm in competition. For example, a permit to a temporary store, a restricted weapon out of residence. This bill seems designed to disarm, over-regu-late and financially devastate the honest Canadian citizen. It will redefine honest Canadians as criminals and punish them severely for things like paper work and storage infractions".
Another constituent writes: "Any reasonable resident of Canada wants to live in a society where violence has been curtailed to an irreducible minimum.
Whereas this bill has been touted as a step in the right direction, in reality it does nothing to support this most worth-while goal. It does not deter criminals from acts of savagery. It does not make access to firearms more difficult for criminals. It does not reduce the propensity toward violence that some members of our society persistently maintain. It does not protect us from members of society who, by virtue of mental illness or the abuse of addictive substances, commit crimes of violence."
Another constituent writes: "My husband and I have been sport shooters and gun owners for several years and as members of the Canadian shooting community are responsible and law-abiding people. Bill C-17 is designed to deceive the public, but it conceals the real purpose, whereby to create laws by non-democratic means, i.e., Order in Council, to confiscate at will millions of dollars worth of legally obtained firearms."
What she is talking about is the fact that when these people bought these firearms-and I do not collect firearms but I understand that these people have a legitimate brief with the government-they have legitimately collected these under the laws of Canada and will not be compensated for giving them back.
She goes on to say that many items of this bill are conceived by bureaucrats and politicians who have absolutely no knowledge of firearms and their use in our society. I think that is what the hon. member from Kenora-Rainy River has been trying to point out throughout this debate.
November 5, 1991

One last quote: "I am sure all non-criminal Canadians would like to see guns out of the hands of criminals and much more severe penalties for the criminal use of firearms. However, the latest Bill C-17 is a typical example of our government in action. Do not identify and tackle the real problem, which is the use of firearms by criminals. Instead, make more regulations in the bureaucracy to harass citizens who are the legitimate owners of firearms".
I think that really sums up my view on this bill. I have tried to point out in debate, and I will tiy it again tomorrow, that I believe very strongly that we need strong gun control and that this bill goes nowhere toward fulfilling that role.

speakeroldname: Mr. Rob Nicholson (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I have just a couple of comments after listening to the hon. member for Haldimand-Norfolk.
He had several problems with the bill and I want to assure him that it is the government's intention to move ahead on the safety provisions. We want to make sure that people who are buying FACs in the future have taken a safety course, are properly certified for the safe handling of firearms, that they have knowledge of the safe storage provisions and that they know the firearms law. These all contribute to a safe and better society, and the government's intention is to move in that direction.
The hon. member said it does nothing for domestic violence. When we get to the prohibition sections, and I believe there is an amendment coming up that will direct hon. members' attention to that, we will see that these are the kinds of things that a judge has to take into consideration when imposing a prohibition order on an individual before the court. I think it is useful in that area.
As well, I am not going to take the time of the House but we have increased penalties across the board. People who commit crimes with firearms are not going to like Bill C-17 because we have upped the penalties all the way along.
Somebody asked me recently: "Why did you not do it for the top crime, robbery?" I said it is life now. You commit robbery with a firearm and the maximum sentence is life. That is the top end under our criminal
Government Orders
justice system. Between that and the minimum sentence we impose of one year, we up the penalties for people who smuggle guns into the country, as I pointed out to the hon. member for Willowdale earlier in the evening, and for people who act in a way that recklessly disregard the safety of others. We have upped the penalties for that. For people who manufacture prohibited weapons, we have upped the penalties right across the board and I think most Canadians are interested in that.
I would like to deal with the specific amendment that the hon. member has.
I know what he is trying to get at. What happens is an individual might come into possession of a firearm and not have an FAC. You may have inherited this firearm if your spouse passed on. It may be a trustee in bankruptcy who might acquire firearms if he seizes the assets of a gun shop that went bankrupt.
The present law now before Parliament says that a person must act with reasonable dispatch either to dispose of the firearms they have come into possession of or get an FAC. We say to act with reasonable dispatch.
The problem that I would have, and I was talking to the hon. member earlier about this, is that if you have a one-year period you create a no man's land. Individuals can, for whatever reason, come into possession of these firearms and can go for a year. They cannot be touched by the police. They do not have to make the effort to do something about that in the same way they are required now.
I hope all members of the House say: "I think the way the government has it here is probably the best way." If you come into possession of these things, you must act with reasonable dispatch to either dispose of the firearms or to get an FAC.
I think it is a better way and as a result I hope the House turns down the suggestion.

Madam Speaker, I wanted to speak very briefly to this proposed amendment because I think it at least places on the record a concern that a number of members on both sides of the House have as to the problem of people coming into possession of firearms, not because they went out and purchased them, but because they came into possession of them simply by operation of law.

Government Orders
Is a gun so evil that simply because it is found in your possession you suddenly become a criminal? Guns by themselves are not so evil that we should be placing that mechanism in law.
I just wanted to quickly point out the several ways-it is not a comprehensive list-that a person can come into possession of a firearm or any other piece of property simply by operation of law.
It could result by way of the execution of a trust whereby the property was put into the hands of a beneficiary. It could happen in the devolution of an estate, either by operation of a will or on an intestacy. It could happen in the movement of property under a bankruptcy. It could happen as a result of a sale in bulk in which a large bulk sale of property took place.
I suppose we could even talk about the ammunition magazine or gun clip that is being prohibited under the legislation now. It could happen when a creditor made a seizure of property where the creditor had a security interest. This could happen in all of the provinces across the country.
I just wanted the record to show that there are a whole lot of instances in which individuals, law-abiding Canadians, could come into possession of guns in a very legal way and they would then be belly-up against provisions of the Criminal Code that could see them charged as breaching provisions of the Criminal Code.
If this legislation is not going to be able to take account of the positions of those law-abiding Canadians then at least the record should show that we had an opportunity to address it here in this House.

Mr. Speaker, I have an amendment to Motion No. 19, clause 9.
It is hoped that this amendment will help the government to see the importance of this particular motion and allow the member for Haldimand-Norfolk's motion to go through.
Basically what we are suggesting is that in (d) we replace "comes into possession of a firearm by operation of law within one year" with "comes into possession of a firearm by operation of law within three months".
It amazes me when I listen to members opposite. Pardon me if I sometimes sound like a constituent of Kenora-Rainy River, but only a lawyer would say that
reasonable dispatch sounds good and is acceptable. If we ask ordinary Canadians out there what that means, they will not know what reasonable dispatch means.
I think it is important when we put legislation forward to the people of Canada that we make it as clear as possible and as simple as possible so that there will be no debate by the local registrar of what is acceptable and what is not acceptable. There are enough words in this legislation that are going to give people a rough time without having to add reasonable dispatch. That could mean in Toronto in about two years from now. In a community like Kenora it could mean two weeks. That is the difference in what we are talking about as far as getting an FAC is concerned and the abilities to check into it.
If we are creating a 28-day waiting period, I think it is important that we put in the allowable time where a person has to go and present themselves to take a course in order that they can keep a particular firearm which may have been given to them by someone such as their father or may have been inherited.
The whole object, I would think, of members opposite and of the government is to get people to want to participate in the process of registering their firearms. I was going to speak on the previous member's intervention on Motion No. 12 by indicating that if they make it so difficult people will just go underground with their firearms and will not bring them in. I think this is a veiy suitable motion and amendment by my colleague because it makes it very clear just how much time someone has.
I have presented the amendment. It is hoped in presenting this amendment to Motion No. 19, which was explained very articulately by my colleague from Haldimand-Norfolk, that the government will see fit to make this very clear change in order for everyone to understand just what it means by reasonable dispatch.

Madam Speaker, I feel like I am being lobbied over here. I just want to remind hon. members how reasonable we were during committee stage, as the member for Cape
November 5, 1991

Breton-The Sydneys will attest in terms of accepting amendments from the opposition.
The only thing I would point out to the member is that I have to disagree because I think most people do know what reasonable dispatch is. I can tell the hon. member why he might not want that. In the example that he gave there might be a situation where a spouse inherits a number of firearms. It may not be reasonable for that person within three months to make the decision to take whatever courses are required and make the necessary applications. It would seem to me that with reasonable dispatch he or she would be in a much better position in satisfying the court, if it ever came to that, in perhaps three or four months. I am not going to get into the argument as to whether it should be two months or six months or anything else. I am just saying to the hon. member that three months is inflexible. I think that with reasonable dispatch is a flexible way of doing it. It may be that a trustee in bankruptcy would have to move in and dispose of a firearm within a few days and three months would be too long. As I say, I can see a situation where a spouse would not be in a position to make the decision immediately to get involved with the courses and regularize his or her position with respect to the firearms.
It was a nice try. I have some sympathy for what the member is saying, but it seems to me the best wording is the wording that we have here: with reasonable dispatch.

Madam Speaker, I do not agree with the parliamentary secretary. I just feel that the amendment suggested by the member for Kenora-Rainy River to this motion is excellent. I think it makes it a very worth-while motion and I think it should be accepted by all parties in the House.
As we have said before, and others have said it, what the government is proposing brings forward a very grey area. What we need is something definitive to be able to reassure Canadians that they have something that they can understand, not something in the mumbo-jumbo that presently exists in the legislation.
I think this is an excellent motion and I think it should be supported.
