speechtext: I remind the House that a vote on Motion No. 20A will apply to Motion No. 23A.

Madam Speaker, I think this is an important motion because we are faced this week with the question of crime prevention.
It seems in the minds of Canadians, the more people we talk to, a concern exists in our country, particularly in our urban areas, about the question of crime prevention. I can remember being in the House last year and speaking on this very point. I talked about crime prevention as did other members in this House. I think it is safe to say that the concern in this country with respect to rising crime rates has increased about 50 per cent in the past year.
I think all Canadians will tell us that the crime rate is increasing. They may not be able to tell us the interest rate of the bank or where the constitutional committee is in any particular week. I do not know if anybody can tell us that. However, I think it is safe to say that one thing they will tell us is that crime is increasing in this country.
It is a concern. It is a concern to everybody. People from coast to coast are being intimidated about the very utilization of the facilities in their own communities, about going in elevators late at night in apartment buildings and about women at this time of the year going home from work when it is dark, getting off a bus and having to walk a block or a block and a half, merely a short distance most of us would say, particularly in the daylight. For women in our cities it is a terror, an absolute terror, and this is not acceptable. Certainly gun control is only one aspect of crime prevention in our country. There are many other aspects, but this is the one with which we are seized this evening.
I think it is important to look at it. The most relevant influence on the increase of crime in our communities is drugs. The increased activity in drugs has made it absolutely imperative that the government not stay in
neutral on the question of crime prevention and that it does something constructive.
Here we are proposing something constructive which can be done to aid the problem, to aid the fight against drugs in our country. We are submitting that the mandatory prohibition of firearms be increased, not just for those who are convicted of an offence of 10 years or more but for those who are convicted of any indictable offence involving violence. This is very significant. If somebody is going to be convicted of an indictable offence involving violence, the fact is that this person is not the type of person we want to be in possession of firearms.
Even more important, we are suggesting that those who are convicted of trafficking in drugs, those who are in possession for the purpose of trafficking and those who are dealing in the export of narcotics and who are convicted of an indictable offence relating to these narcotics and drugs, should also be prohibited from using a firearm.
For the first offence it should be 10 years. For the second offence it should be life. This requires a great deal of circumspection by those who would be prone to deal in drugs. When they know they are going to lose the right to the use of a firearm for 10 years in the first instance and for life in the second, then certainly they will be much more prudent about their actions. Not only that, but we have seen in drug related offences that sometimes where a person is convicted of more than one offence at subsequent times the actual convictions escalate in their seriousness.
What we were saying is that if we can in the first instance on a conviction of an indictable offence relating to drugs prohibit the use of a firearm by that person, we may actually prohibit the fact that the person may commit a subsequent crime using a firearm.
I think that is very important. But it also gives a great deal of assurance to people in our communities that the drug activity will not continue to escalate at the rate it has in the recent past.
I think the Criminal Code already requires all firearms dealers to make note of this as well. In particular, drug gangs make it advisable and justifiable to ensure that all those convicted of any violent indictable offence will be subject to a prohibition order on the possession of firearms or ammunition.
November 5, 1991

Now discretionary orders may be favoured by judges but they require that the Crown and judges put their minds to the question of a prohibition order and take a sufficiently serious view of the need for such orders.
A mandatory order ensures that the order will be made and that there will not be that discretion. I am not as a rule in favour of mandatory orders because I think the discretion should be left with the judiciary. However in this case we are dealing with and really fighting a rearguard action against organized crime and particularly drug related crimes in our cities. This is the least serious infringement on the normal relation that the judge can have with the accused and we are impinging just a little on the discretionary powers of the judges.
When you consider what is at stake I think it is absolutely necessary. Mandatory prohibition orders should apply to all drug trafficking offences when they are serious enough to be prosecuted as indictable offences. Minor offences will be dealt with as summary conviction matters. We are not talking about casual dealings in drugs. The nature of the offence alone might justify a mandatory prohibition order, but given the incidence of firearms use by drug gangs in the cities, the argument is even stronger.
It is difficult to imagine a case in which a conviction for an indictable offence involving violence or drug trafficking would not merit a prohibition order on the possession of firearms.
Bill C-17 would provide the discretion necessary to make exceptions in appropriate cases. Proposed new subsections (1.1) to (1.3) would give the judge a discretion not to make the order where the circumstances of the particular offender and the particular offence made that appropriate; where the offender needed a firearm in order to provide sustenance or where the effect of such an order would make it impossible for the person to hold employment.
This will provide an escape valve for aboriginals and other persons who may have a special need for a firearm and who despite the conviction for an indictable offence do not appear to pose a danger to the public.
We have tried every way possible to make this motion applicable to those who need an exception but we must in all conscience do something about the increasing crime rate in the communities in this country. We
Government Orders
cannot turn away from the fact that drug related offences are increasing and something has to be done.
We therefore submit this motion in the hope that the government will accept it and really put some action behind their so-called stated inclination to favour crime prevention in this country. It is one thing to talk about crime prevention but it is quite another to back it up and to do something that the people in this country are crying out for.
I would ask the government to put a little action behind their declarations.

Madam Speaker, I would like to speak on this motion on behalf of the New Democratic Party.
A week or so ago I visited the Port Coquitlam hunting and fishing club high up in the north shore mountains overlooking the Fraser Valley. They have a wonderful club house there. We discussed this bill. I tried to explain how I would support this bill because I was in favour of effective gun control. I tried to make sure as much as possible that they would not be unreasonably affected by bureaucratic measures that would hurt them. They accepted that Canadians are generally in favour of stronger and more effective gun control, especially in light of the massacres and the growing misuse of firearms.
I tried to explain that the bill would try to catch people who were deranged. These people would have to apply for a firearms acquisition certificate before they could buy a gun. We could perhaps weed these people out since they had to have references before they got the gun.
I tried to explain that we would also, through the safe storage provisions of the bill, try to stop people who were momentarily depressed and deranged or teenagers and so on, from grabbing the family gun and killing themselves or other people in their family.
They listened. Sometimes they did not agree with me entirely but they listened and I listened to them in return.
The point that was made over and over again was to get tough on criminals, get tough on the criminal misuse of guns.

November 5, 1991
Government Orders
Having listened to that I am pleased to support these two amendments tonight. I understand that the first amendment would prohibit anyone convicted of a serious drug trafficking offence from owning a firearm for 10 years. We know that with criminal gangs, and especially in drug trafficking, firearms are used and it will be tough to crack down on that with this amendment. We should not kid ourselves that this is going to end that but we can recognize it in the legislation.
The other amendment, as I understand it, extends the ban on firearms possession to anyone convicted of a violent crime, not just those sentenced to 10 years or more. A repeat offender would face a lifetime ban. I would support that. I think I have made some similar proposals in committee. I was listening to what the member said and I was listening to what the hunting and fishing clubs in my riding said and I accept that.
I was worried about persons up north, native persons, who might have an incident in town and then in the cold light of day suddenly be faced with a ban on a gun needed to hunt for food to feed himself or the family.
As I understand it, that is protected in the bill because there is an exception for sustenance.
I was a former Crown attorney for the city of Vancouver. I have been defence counsel. In my experience judges did give tough sentences to people who used firearms in the commission of offences.
I think if these amendments are put in this bill, they would give the clear message that we are also concerned as a Parliament with the criminal misuse of firearms.
I want to conclude by saying that I support this amendment. A week or so ago, I said to the government: "We really need a package for effective gun control that will include a fair registration system, looking at ammunition, looking at really safe storage provisions, looking at getting rid of these converted semi-automatics and these kind of paramilitary weapons and at the same time protect the legitimate hunters and competition shooters". I think we have moved toward that. I really do. I think we are moving toward that now. We also want to give the message that the criminal use of firearms will be hit.
I predict that in the near future we will see such pressure coming from Canadians, especially in the big
cities, that there will be further measures I hope on the misuse of the handgun. This bill doesn't really deal with the hand gun. I tried to get it in the bill through some amendments, but it is basically out of the bill. It peripherally deals with the hand gun when we deal with clip size, but it really doesn't. We are going to have to do that because of the growing use of hand guns by the criminal element in our cities. We are going to have to get even tougher there. One way we can do that is to signal through these two amendments that for criminal offences, criminal types will have to pay an additional penalty by being prohibited in the future as part of their sentences from possessing a firearm.

Mr. Speaker, I have a few comments on the amendment proposed by the member for Cape Breton-The Sydneys.
This particular amendment does not impact at all on the law-abiding gun owner. We have to recognize in the large cities now the proximity of guns to drug trafficking. It is a very real phenomenon in the big cities. In my view lying behind this amendment the logic is precise, the sanction is precise, and it places the burden of the sanction squarely on the shoulders of the serious offender, the drug trafficker.
There is no need to burden a judge or a busy Crown Attorney with the challenge of recommending a certain type of suspension or not, the precision is there in the act, if it is there. I feel that this would take us a lot closer to placing the burden of gun control or at least the penalties for breaches on the shoulders of those who break our criminal laws.

speakeroldname: Mr. Rob Nicholson (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the first point I would like to make is that this bill carries a mandatory prohibition for any indictable offence involving the use, threat or attempt of violence if the maximum sentence available is 10 years or more, a mandatory sentence that says that if you are convicted of a crime of that nature that you cannot possess, own use a firearm for 10 years. That is mandatory.
On the other indictable offences all the government is saying is that the judge must direct his or her attention to the advisability in that case of whether a firearm prohibition should be imposed.


The hon. member who introduced this motion said there was an escape valve. He made the point that he agrees that discretion should be left in the hands of the judges and he pointed out the escape valve. I can tell him that that escape valve is very narrow. In fact, I do not think it would include the situation that is taking place in our territories where if a young native person gets involved with trafficking in narcotics, gets involved with drugs, there are sentences that have been imposed by judges where they can get reintegrated into their culture and sent out of the town, away from the problem area, and they are required to use firearms as part of the native's learning life skills program. I do not think that would be covered, quite frankly, in the exception that the hon. member pointed out in the bill.
The other problem I see with it is this. Some times a court will proceed by indictment for something like common assault, and there are hundreds, I suppose thousands, of those kinds of convictions in a year. I cannot honestly say that it is always appropriate in every circumstance that in every common assault case that is proceeded by way of indictable offence that a 10-year mandatory prohibition against the use of firearms is appropriate. To this extent I agree with the mover that, yes, we should leave the discretion with the judge.
The final point I want to make to the hon. member- he knows, he is a lawyer and so is the member for Port Moody-Coquitlam-is that if you do not give the judge the discretion, the discretion wall be somewhere else. I ask the member to consider this. If the Crown Attorney is thinking of laying an indictable charge, many times he will not with something like this because the penalty would be way out of line to the crime committed. You would be taking the discretion away from the judge and, in a sense, you would be asking the Crown Attorney to make up his or her mind whether they will go by indictable offence or not.
On the three counts, I think it would unnecessarily hurt a good program that is taking place in the Northwest Territories. I think it takes the discretion away from the judge when he or she should have it in terms of say an indictable offence for common assault as well as the other reasons that I have mentioned.
Government Orders
I think the House should turn this down.

Mr. Speaker, I would like to speak specifically to Motion No. 20 with respect to the drug trafficking offences.
I, too, have spoken to many people in my riding regarding this bill. I spoke to many hunters and people who are involved in shooting clubs. They have indicated to me that one of the things this government, this country and judges should be doing is getting tougher on the criminal element in this country.
With respect to Motion No. 20, that would prohibit anyone convicted of a serious drug or trafficking offence from owning a firearm for 10 years, I think that is a very good amendment to be added to the legislation. Certainly in large urban centres where drug trafficking is a very serious offence and many times there is violence involved, it has caused a lot of emotion and a lot of pain and suffering.
If we are going to have gun laws that are going to be reasonable and are going to have some effect, we need to have some very tough laws. I would certainly support the amendment with respect to drug traffickers receiving a 10-year ban on any use of any firearm. That is something that goes a long way to sending a message to drug offenders and also to the courts, because there has been some concern that all of the courts have tended to be tough on offences where violence is used and where weapons are used. There are instances where this has not been the case and I think it is important for this body to send a message to the courts throughout this land that in fact we want the courts to be tough. We want the courts to have some impact on these violent offenders.
I would therefore support this particular amendment.

speakeroldname: Mr. Dave Worthy (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Public Works):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Public Works
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would like to speak very briefly on this.
I know that I and many others in this House have been very strong on the law and order aspects of this bill. The people across the country, as well as most of the people in the House, recognize that we have not sent a strong enough signal to those who misuse firearms, and we want to do that.

Government Orders
On the surface, this motion seems to address that and, in most people's minds, it should be an acceptable one for people who take the law and order stance that I have taken.
Not being a lawyer, I do not get into all of the legal frills in this type of a motion but what it means as a motion to me and to the people I represent. We have in this bill now charged that judges will have to review people who are guilty of the offences that we are talking about. They are charged with making the decision as to whether or not there should be a prohibition order placed on their possession of guns. That is much stronger than we have now. The judge in doing that review can tell the difference between somebody on the fringes of a drug gang in one of the cities or possibly a native on the DEW line of Canada who happens to have been involved in school with some relatively innocent sale of drugs, let us say marijuana.
There is a big difference between violence in crime or the real violence that we see in so many situations across the country and in many cases a rancher who may only get into the city two or three times a year. Unfortunately, unless he has had a good fight, he would not have a good reason to come back to the city.
This type of amendment would in fact sweep these people into the same net as the criminals and the violent people who we really are trying to address. In my opinion the discretion of the judge or the fact that we are charging the judge to review and make that decision is adequate.

That Bill C-17 be amended in clause 27 by striking out line 40 at

He said: Mr. Speaker, let me try to explain to the House what is happening here. As I said before, most of this bill is in regulations. For example, safe storage, clip size and so on. We wanted to get a system whereby there would be fair regulations and I think that is important.
I would prefer that the minister would give us all the regulations now. We should have the regulations before the bill, or around about the bill rather than after the bill, but that is the way things seem to work. We are getting them after the bill.
As we understand it, the regulations will be vetted by this Firearms Advisory Committee, with people who are knowledgeable about weapons, guns and firearms and so on. They will be vetting the regulations.
There was a proposal put in the original bill by the government that there would be a negative resolution by the House, so the House itself, so MPs could get a look at the regulations. That was withdrawn and rather an extraordinary member of the legislative committee, the government Whip, made a proposal that any committee
Government Orders
of the House of Commons could undertake an investigation and do a report on any firearms regulation. This brings in a very interesting proposal. A member or some members who did not like a regulation could get that regulation examined by a committee of the House. But it says: "any committee of the House."
It seems to me-and I think hon. members opposite would agree with this-that this is a bit too far open. This is what you would call in constitutional terms an egregious error perhaps. It is too broad. Does "any committee" mean that if a few members dislike the clip size, for example, they will try to get it in the justice committee, but if the justice committee says no, we dealt with that, then they will go to the agricultural committee or they will go to the defence committee? I mean, you could literally go committee shopping until you got a sympathetic committee chair or a committee you could get some control of, and you could get it in the committee. You could have an agricultural committee on the basis that farmers use a gun for whatever reason, and if you could get it on and you get the right chair and the right person, you could get it in that committee. You could committee shop and go around.
What my amendment does is say we will accept that provision that the House can scrutinize those amendments, but let us put it in the Standing Committee on Justice, let us make it reasonable. I think that is a fair trade-off and I think that is a reasonable way of handling it. After all, we are talking about firearms. We are talking about amendments to a bill, to the Criminal Code. It should be done by the Standing Committee on Justice. Let us say an out of order amendment, an out of order regulation, a kind of wild regulation got through the screening of the firearms committee, which is going to be pretty hard. But if even got through that, it could go to the justice committee and MPs would get feedback.
MPs who get feedback, not bureaucrats or appointees but MPs who are responsible to constituents, could then examine it. They should do it in the justice committee. Does that not make sense?
It does not make sense to me to move it all around different committees, and that is why I propose this amendment.

speechtext:
Motion No. 50.
That Bill C-17 be amended by striking out line 5 at page 36 and
substituting the following new clause:
"28. The said Act is further amended by adding thereto,
immediately after section 116 thereof, the following section:
"116.1 (1) Every order made by the Governor in Council under any provision of this Part shall be laid before each House of Parliament by a member of the Queen's Privy Council for Canada not later than five sitting days after it is made.
(2)	Where an order has been laid before Parliament pursuant to subsection (1), a motion for the consideration of either House, to the effect that the order be revoked, signed by not less than twenty members of the House of Commons in the case of a motion for the consideration of that House and by not less than fifteen members of the Senate in the case of a motion for the consideration of the Senate may be filed with the Speaker of the appropriate House at any time but not later than twenty sitting days after the regulation has been laid before that House.
(3)	Where a motion is filed as provided in subsection (2), the House in which the motion was filed shall, not later than its sixth sitting day following the filing of the motion, take up and consider the motion, unless a motion to the like effect has earlier been taken up and considered in the other House.
(4)	A motion taken up and considered in accordance with subsection (3) shall be debated without interruption for not more than one hour and, on the conclusion of the debate or at the expiration of that hour, the Speaker of the House of Commons or the Senate, as the case may be, shall immediately put every question necessary for the disposition of the motion.
(5)	If a motion taken up and considered in accordance with subsection (3) is adopted, with or without amendments, a message shall be sent from the House adopting the motion informing the other House that the motion has been so adopted and requesting that the motion be concurred in by that other House.
November 5, 1991

(6)	Within the first fifteen sitting days next after receipt by it of a request pursuant to subsection (5), that House shall take up and consider the motion that is the subject of the request, and all questions in connection with the motion shall be debated without interruption for not more than one hour and, on the conclusion of the debate or at the expiration of that hour, the Speaker of the House of Commons or the Senate, as the case may be, shall immediately put every question necessary to determine whether or not the motion in question is concurred in.
(7)	Where a motion taken up and considered in accordance with this section is adopted, with or without amendements, by the House in which it was introduced and is concurred in by the other House, the order to which the motion relates shall stand revoked.

He said: Mr. Speaker, this follows on the previous amendment. It would be an alternative to the previous amendment and one which I personally would favour.
One of the great concerns that I have with this bill is that so much of this bill is done through regulations. We are passing a bill that in many ways is enabling and gives the minister carte blanche to do what he or she may wish to do with respect to huge portions of this bill.
We have in this country today, I would suggest, a problem in that we are increasingly being controlled by decisions in cabinet and by regulations. That is a problem that has been ongoing, certainly, since I came here as a member. There have been a number of times when I have been frustrated by the fact that my voice either cannot be heard or counts for very little. The bill before us today simply adds to that. That has existed in other legislation.
Recently on Bill C-13, the Canadian Bar Association was before that legislative committee indicating that it thought there was too much regulation in the country. An individual has a tough time getting hold of the statutes and regulations to know what the law should be.
It is important that parliamentarians have a say in what takes place in this country. That is what we are elected to do. There certainly is a place for regulations.
Government Orders
This bill talks of the storage and handling of weapons by owners, people who are in the business of selling guns. The shipping, the handling, the storage and sale of those weapons are all handled strictly in regulations. The size of the gun magazine is handled strictly in regulations. The regulations have not been presented to this House to let us debate them, to let us see exactly what they are. We are in the dark with this bill. Therefore we are passing legislation and we are not really sure where it is going to end up. That is the concern of people throughout the country who have some interest in this bill.
This amendment would bring back a clause in the original bill that would force the government to bring any regulations in front of the House to be debated and to be voted upon. That way they would be in front of the Canadian public. It would allow members who wish to put a case for or against a certain regulation to put that case and would allow us, as members, to have a vote and a say in the regulation.
This is an alternative to the previous amendment but it is one that I would prefer. I suggest it is something that is important if we, as parliamentarians, are going to truly represent our various constituencies.

speakeroldname: Mr. Rob Nicholson (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the hon. member made some interesting comments about the role of the private member and some of the frustrations he has had concerning amendments and the shaping of legislation.
I say with some com iction that this bill is not one of those bills. I can tell the hon. member that individual members of Parliament have made a difference. Compare this bill to the way it was originally tabled in June 1989, and the changes that were made after the Reimer committee and the many recommendations that were made by a committee of this House. When this bill went before the legislative committee it was changed.
The very amendment that the hon. member is suggesting be put back in the bill is an amendment that came out of the committee process. His colleague, the member for Port Moody-Coquitlam, will remember that. I was there as a witness with the departmental officials

Government Orders
onbehalf of the Minister of Justice. This was not an amendment I came up with. This came from members of the committee.
You can point out that it was a Conservative member of the committee, but I can tell you it was not something I drew up and thought would be a great idea. The committee thought it would be a good way of handling regulations.
I can tell the hon. member with some certainty that there is no other provision in the laws of Canada that provides parliamentarians with this opportunity to debate and study regulations before the regulations get into the process by which they become law. It is usually too late by the time parliamentarians think they might want to get interested in this. By that time the thing has been published and is well along the road. This is unique, I believe, in the whole body of law and all the regulations passed by the Government of Canada, going right straight back to the beginning of regulations.
This provides an opportunity for parliamentarians to have a look at it before it has the opportunity to have the force of law.
I see what the hon. member is doing. He is saying that he did like it the way it was previous to that, but we tried to come up with a balance and, in a sense, we would be open to the charge that: "You did not listen to your own committee. Your own committee backed this." I could be corrected on this, but I think it was unanimously accepted. I do not see anybody shaking their head. I believe this procedure for having a look at regulations was unanimously accepted. As I say, at the time it was not my first choice as to the way it should be done but I can see where this is a dramatic improvement over the way it was done in the past.
I say, with some reluctance, that I will not be supporting going back, but I think there are lots of benefits here for the individual member in the way this is now worded.

Mr. Speaker,I just wanted to add something to what the parliamentary secretarysaid. We are trying to strike a balance, but one of the fears that Ihave is that it is very controversial, as you might have guessed, when a regulation is made concerning clip size, safe storage and thetypes of para-military guns that are banned. What happens then is itgoes through the firearms advisory
committee and then maybe a memberof the House with some pressure, who has a right, tries to get Preferred to a committee.
I am a little afraid that the process will still be delayed and that nothing may ever happen. That is why I was very reluctant when the member for Calgary proposed this process. I cannot look into the future because I do not have a crystal ball so we will wait to see what happens.
Will it work or will it be a vehicle for undetermined delay and debate of the same issues that we have been debating for the last year and a half? We want to get on with the thing so that we have some sort of idea of just what exactly is controlled and what is not. We do not want to have a mechanism that is a recipe for delay and delay.
Maybe the government is a little afraid to bring it in. It is delayed, examined, Parliament was not sitting, an election comes, and so on and so forth. Having said we had better get on with it, I will sit down and let us do that in the House.

speakeroldname: Mr. Russell MacLellan (Cape Breton-The Sydneys) moved:
speechtext:
Motion No. 59
That Bill C-17 be amended in clause 38
(a)	by striking out line 39 at page 43 and substituting the following therefor:
"the case may be, is carried on;"
(b)	by striking out line 45 at page 43 and substituting the following therefor:
"the Commissioner or person so authorized; and
(e) mail copies of the records of all retail sales transactions involving firearms to the local registrar of firearms within fifteen days of the end of each calendar month."

Motion No. 60
That Bill C-17 be amended in clause 38 by striking out lines 41 to 45 at page 43 and substituting the following therefor:
"tory relating to restricted weapons and firearms to the Commissioner or to any person authorized by subsection 110(5) to issue a permit to carry on a business in accordance with any request made in writing by the Commissioner or that person so authorized or such requirements as are defined by regulation."

Mr. Speaker, this is an amendment which I think can have a good deal of importance because it will be a beginning of registration. I think that the main complaint to the request by the pro-gun control groups to registration of all firearms is that it would create an overload of activity for the officials. There would be so much information to program into the computer in a very short period of time that really the whole system of registration and controls and inquiries concerning FACs and so on would not work well.
The important thing is that when we try to make the system more effective and increase the regulation and control, we do not overload it so that the whole system breaks down.
What we are suggesting in Motion No. 59 is that the retail sales be the point at which we start with some registration. The person who completes the retail sale mails copies of all retail sales transactions involving firearms to the local registrar of firearms within 15 days of the end of each calendar month. Those records of firearms with the registration number and so on would then be put on a computer and we would have the
Government Orders
beginning of the registration of firearms. That would put the system in place for the registration of firearms.
Mind you it would involve some work to get the system going. If it is the intention to eventually register all firearms, this would be the manner in which this registration could be started. I think it is a modest beginning but one which could work without overloading the system and overtaxing the activities and the time of the officials. They also have to do research and make inquiries on FAC applications and renewals. They have to deal with the registration of hand guns, deal with amnesties and other inquiries. I think this would be a suitable means of adding to the registration program.

Mr. Speaker, I wish to speak on my Motion No. 60, which would place on obligation on a firearms business to record all retail sales and send the information to the RCMP. At present they only have to send records of sales of restricted weapons.
I just want to take a moment and deal with the restricted weapons. I meant to mention this before on a debate on one of the motions and it fits in here. What are restricted weapons? They are hand guns; they are semi-automatic firearms with barrels shorter than 470 millimetres; they are any rifle or shotgun that can be fired while its stock is folded or telescoped; automatic weapons grandfathered in 1977 and any weapon declared by cabinet order to be a restricted weapon.
By far the largest group is hand guns. I just looked at the Metro Tbronto Police Board testimony because we have been hearing a lot about crime in Tbronto. They came before our committee and this is what they said: "It is not commonly known by most Canadians that when a registration certificate is issued for a restricted weapon it is valid for life". I draw to the attention of the committee that surely things can change in a lifetime and we should re-evaluate that. The certificates are issued free of charge. It is estimated by the Metropolitan Toronto Police Force that it costs about a thousand dollars to conduct an investigation into an application for a restricted weapon, usually a hand gun. A thousand bucks to look at it. Surely the time has arrived for a user fee. They point out that there are strong points in the legislation that can be improved, and so on.

Government Orders
Then they give us some statistics. I think this is really interesting. It is fitting perhaps that we end the debate tonight with this: restricted weapons certificates 1986, 33,200; 1987, 37,500; 1990, 46,000 new registrations. Metro police say that the number in Toronto has grown exponentially and in 1991 three times as many were issued as previously. People are getting certificates for hand guns.
They can get them to use as protection, in a lawful occupation, as target practice, as part of a shooting club and part of a collection of a genuine gun collector. You can start off with one gun. Hand guns do not really have any hunting purposes. Some are incredibly powerful and they can be concealed.
Someone who sees the Dirty Harry film and wants toown a Colt 44 magnum like the hero of the film can go to the libraryand learn about magnums. He can then go to his local registry office to get his restricted weapon certificate. He can get one based on the fact that he says he is a genuine gun collector. He buys the weaponand keeps it in his home.
Metro Toronto police are telling us that the number of people doing this is growing like crazy. It is the Rambo culture. This is a serious problem and there is really nothing in the bill to deal with it.
What the member for Cape Breton-The Sydneys and myself have been saying to the House and the Canadian people is: "Let us target these hand guns and then get back to these para-militaiy weapons". These are not for hunters. These are para-militaiy weapons that are flowing into Canada. We are saying that when people buy guns surely with modern cash registers and computers and things we can take a record and send it to the RCMP.
People will say this is a tremendous violation of civil rights. Is it when you weigh everything? The member for Saint-Hubert said: "We don't have the third amendment that gives us the right to have a weapon". This country was settled peacefully. We have hunting guns and so on, but by and large good hunters do not need powerful weapons. We do not have any elephants in our woods in Canada. Inuit used to shoot polar bears with bow and arrow and spears.
We do not need these high powered guns. We do not need them flooding into this country. We need some controls.
I think what the member for Cape Breton-The Sydneys is doing with his amendment and what I am trying to do with my amendment is point to the future. That will be the big debate in Canada in the future. Can we have a registration system for future guns so we know where they are and how armed our population is so that if they are lost, stolen or get into criminal hands, we can deal with them?
It seems to me that is where it is going to go in the future. I think people have to be prepared for that. I urge the government to accept our amendments.

speakeroldname: Mr. Dave Worthy (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Public Works):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Public Works
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would like to address the specific amendments that are being proposed here. They were addressed in committee. There was a lot of discussion on them. Of course, there was a lot of discussion across the country generally about the value and the problems of registration.
There is a terrible fear by some people of the process of registration for all guns. Yet there is a terrible demand by many others who feel that is the way we should be going in the future.
I will not attempt to argue whether we should or we should not. I will argue that we are now with this bill going to be vastly increasing the number of weapons that are registered and therefore under better control. I think most people in Canada feel that is positive.
The special committee studying Bill C-80 recommended that in fact we should be going far beyond these automatic and automatics converted to semi-automatic.
There is a whole culture of guns not legitimately used by hunters or sporting people. We in that committee felt that people in Canada, not all people in Canada, but the majority of the people, were insisting that we address that issue.
The concern is what to do with those that are already in the country and what to do with those that have been legitimately bought by law-abiding people. The committee made recommendations on that but this bill does not directly address those.
I would be disappointed if most of those guns do not end up onthe registry as restricted weapons, weapons that are owned by people in the country, known by the

November 5, 1991
police and under control.This will vastly increase the number of registered weapons. It willtend to include all of those that are now in the country and what wewould determine as the higher fire power type weapons.
We are not saying to go back to all the old guns that are in the country, but to the new ones that are being brought in. It is a very attractive, I will even use the word seductive, approach. It seems so simple and so easy.
As I pointed out to the committee, in one of my former lives I was a computer consultant involved very heavily with computers and computer systems. If you are going to implement a computer system it has to be something that can be maintained accurately or you are going to end up with garbage. It is something that everybody recognizes but it is a trap that is easy to fall into.
This is a trap that the House is being asked to consider now. Ifall new sales are put into a computer there is no demand that thoserecords be maintained. If a person moves there is no record required of that move. If a person who legally owns a gun sells it to anotherperson who has a firearms acquisition certificate there is no reasonfor them to send that record to the computer system. In very shortorder that system, and a very expensive computer system by the way,would be full of data and a significant percentage of it would begarbage. As such, the whole system really becomes useless.
The concept of paying a lot of taxpayer money in trying to develop a safer system when that system would be invalid would detract from many of the other good things we are doing in the bill. Although it is a seductive motion, and the idea is one that would appeal to many people, I would strongly recommend to the House that it not accept this amendment.

speakeroldname: Mr. Peter L. McCreath (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of State (Finance and Privatization)):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of State (Finance and Privatization)
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I just want to add a few brief comments, if I may. I have sat quietly throughout the discussion and on this particular amendment I could not help but find myself in the position of agreeing with virtually everything my hon. friend from Port Moody-Coquitlam said.
However, I find myself unable to support the amendment and I want to say why.
Government Orders
This is one of those issues that is a very, very difficult issue and it has been difficult for members on all sides of the house. I think it has been approached in a very constructive way by members on all sides. As I read the many amendments that were put forward here today, I was impressed with the thought that had gone into them.
There were some that in some ways I agreed with and others that I did not. It is difficult achieving a consensus on this issue. We went through Bill C-80 in the special committee. We went through the committee that handled Bill C-17. All members of the House, while they may not find that the bill provides everything they are looking for, would agree that this minister and her parliamentary secretary who is here, have really bent over backward to try to find a fair and reasonable path between two competing points of view on this very, very difficult issue.
I represent a rural area. I have never owned a gun and I likely never will own a gun. I found that when this gun control issue first came up, in 90 per cent of the households in my constituency there were firearms. As I watched this issue unfold and tried to find out the concerns of the people I represent, one of the things I found was that there was a real urban split on this issue.
I found that it almost seemed to hurt the rural Canadians, at least the ones in Atlantic Canada, so that they were almost under assault on this issue, as if to own a firearm made you some sort of closet Rambo who wanted to go out and do vicious, evil and violent things. That is not the way people are in rural Nova Scotia.
People in rural Nova Scotia are responsible. I am very pleased that the various gun clubs in my constituency and many of my constituents who have written to me on this issue are very responsible in their approach. They are going to welcome some of the provisions in this bill.
They did not look to the government to bring in a bill of this sort, but they are reasonable people and they will see some of the provisions like the 28-day delay, for example, and the requirement for training for new people. Some of these very responsible provisions have been a constructive contribution.
There are very legitimate concerns that have been expressed to me by a number of my constituents about things like what will be in the regulations that will follow. I am pleased to see that any regulations will be com-

Government Orders
ingbefore committee before they in fact are promulgated. This is one of the big concerns.
With regard to the state of the motion before the House, which is the amendments-I know you wish me to do that-and the point I want to make is that a lot of members have participated in the exercise that has got this bill to where it is.
There was give and take on both sides of the issue. The minister is to be commended for her willingness to listen and to try to accommodate the different points of view that exist. As with any difficult issue, compromise is necessary and the bill that is ultimately brought before the House at this time represents a compromise that is probably as reasonable as can be had. It offers something to everybody who has an interest in the bill without necessarily giving everything to everyone.
That is why I am not going to support the current amendment that is before the House, but wish to commend the bill in its final stage to all members. I think all members should be prepared to support it.

speakeroldname: Mr. Rob Nicholson (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I do not want to belabour the point because I think it has been covered by my colleague.
I just want to point out that in fact there is some control, and I think it is done in a less expensive, less elaborate manner than might have been suggested by the two amendments here.
A firearms dealer is required to record the serial number and the FAC number of purchases. Police can have a look at that. Indeed, that was one of the ways they identified Marc Lepine. They checked the serial number on his gun, and they checked it against the FAC in the place where he bought it.
I can tell the hon. member from the New Democratic Party that even if we were going to accept it, he would probably want to add prohibited weapons which can be in the inventory of a company.
His amendment refers to restricted weapons. If we were going to accept it, we would have to put "prohibited". I do not mean to be picky, but as I say, the system
in place is inexpensive and it is easy for the police to get at.
The hon. member from British Columbia just pointed out that we would have garbage very quickly because this does not put any requirement on private citizens who have a transaction. There is no requirement on them to have that recorded, so very quickly you would find that the records you have are completely out of date. You would have incurred this huge expense to very little advantage.
As much as I would like to have accepted an amendment from the member, I do not think that is possible.

Mr. Speaker, I just want to put on the record my support for the concept in general, but it is impossible to do in this bill as we found at the committee stage, as my friend from Cariboo-Chilcotin pointed out.
It is there with this bill. Everything is in position for a future minister to take the next logical step which will be a total revision of part III of the Criminal Code which will pull in those parts that this bill did not deal with.
Members who served on the committee know that part III has 33 sections to it. This bill only dealt with 24 of those sections. Before we can move into these newer concepts, a minister has to bring all of part III before the bill and then a minister may well decide to get into a licensing and registration system where, depending on your degree of training, you will be able to have access to certain guns and not other guns. It will be treated more like cars. You will have a proper licence. If you are going to be a chauffeur you will have a better type of licence. You will have different insurance ratings.
Everything has to be done as a package. This bill has to be done first because we have to get all of those training courses in place before we can take the next step. It is with regret I say that because I know the member has worked very hard on it. Mr. Speaker, perhaps you would permit me to have a word because I had the privilege of

November 5, 1991

chairing that committee. Being as these are the last amendments, I want the record to show clearly in terms of the government members that the member for Cariboo-Chilcotin, the member for Red Deer and the member for Ahuntsic all worked very hard. In terms of the Liberals, the member for Cape Breton-The Sydneys worked very hard on this bill and very productively. My good friend from Port Moody-Coquitlam really did work hard. It was a treat to put a group of members around a bill that was very sensitive across the country and within this Parliament and to have them work constructively.
Of course it cannot be done without a parliamentary secretary, the member for Niagara Falls, who worked very hard, and then the minister. I mean we all remember being years and years in this House in opposition when we could not get an amendment through at all. It was frustrating for the Liberal members when they were on the back benches, but in the last 10 years, starting under the Liberal Party in 1980 and continuing through with the Conservative Party, committees now have awesome powers and make some very significant amendments to bills.
This gives us satisfaction. I want to say that it takes a minister who is not psyched out by a committee and who is prepared to listen to the rational arguments that are made. There are rational arguments made, and the Minister of Justice deserves a lot of credit for the amendments that she accepted both to Bill C-17 and to Bill C-80.
